item.title: Seahawks vs. Broncos 'Thursday Night Football' betting odds, picks and predictions: Best bets, player props
item.description: Our NFL handicapper break downs his favorite bets in the Seahawks-Broncos matchup on "Thursday Night Football."
item.content:encoded:
The temperature should rise on a chilly Thursday night when the Denver Broncos welcome the Seattle Seahawks to Empower Field at Mile High for their prime-time showdown.

This matchup features franchises looking to find some consistency heading into the middle part of the season. Seattle (3-2) comes to town fresh off a disappointing 32-29 home defeat at the hands of the undefeated San Francisco 49ers. Quarterback Sam Darnold had a rough night, connecting on just 18-of-29 passes for 195 yards and a touchdown. He was also picked off twice.

On the other side, Denver (3-2) recorded a 23-17 road triumph against the winless Los Angeles Chargers in Week 5. Head coach Sean Payton saw his team, led by quarterback Bo Nix and running back J.K. Dobbins, rebound nicely following its Week 4 setback against San Francisco.

Let's take a deep dive into this game and see where we've uncovered betting value.

Seattle Seahawks (-2.5, 40.5) at Denver Broncos

On paper, the one thing that stands out is the contrast in defenses.

Seattle is an absolute juggernaut, ranking No. 1 in total defense at a paltry 1,256 yards. The Seahawks sit atop the league in passing yards allowed (754) and 11th overall in rushing yards conceded (502) this season.

In contrast, Denver hasn't been close to those numbers thus far. The Broncos are 23rd in total defense (1,737 yards), 11th in passing yards (1,011) and a dismal 30th in rushing yards allowed overall (726).

Making matters worse for Denver: Standout cornerback Patrick Surtain will miss Thursday's game with an ankle injury, which means it could be open season on the Denver secondary for Darnold, star wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Co.

Offensively, Seattle has been scoring points at will of late. After a season-opening 13-10 win against the New England Patriots, the Seahawks have scored at least 29 points in their last four games.

As for Denver, Nix and his offense will be up against it. Despite the record, Nix has been mediocre at best this season. He has failed to reach 135 passing yards in two of five games, leading to a subpar 80.8 passer rating that falls short (87.8) of his 2025 number in the metric.

If there's one thing working for Denver, though, it's the consistency in delivering big-time performances at home. The Broncos are 10-2 at home during the regular season over their last two campaigns, including wins against Super Bowl contenders — Jacksonville Jaguars and the Los Angeles Rams — this year.

Putting all of that information together, I'm getting creative with a Same Game Parlay to find a little bit of value. I think this affair stays close and will likely come down to a field goal or last-minute scoring drive to decide it, so I'm landing on Denver to cover the key alternate number and the total to clear 36.5 points.

That gets us plus money on the play, which I'm happy to take in what should be a nip-and-tuck game in Denver.

Bet: Same Game Parlay: Denver +3.5 and over 36.5 (+147, Caesars)

Player props

RB Emanuel Wilson: 2+ receptions (-118) | 3+ receptions (+240) | 4+ receptions (+580) and over 80.5 rushing + receiving yards (-114) at FanDuel

Everyone is talking about Wilson having a big night on the ground against the Denver defense. And that might be the case.

However, I think folks are sleeping on the fourth-year man out of Fort Valley State in the receiving game. Darnold is going to feel the heat from the Broncos' defense, which means his time in the pocket will be limited. He was sacked five times in the loss to San Francisco, so I expect offensive coordinator Brian Fleury to utilize Wilson in the passing game.

We're playing one of our fun ladder plays with Wilson. He has had at least two catches in that last two games, highlighted by 22 total touches and playing 60% of Seattle's snaps against San Francisco.

I'm also backing Wilson to clear the number of combined rushing/receiving yards. Denver has conceded 145 rushing yards per game, (fourth most), so he will be active in all facets of the Seahawks offense.

TE AJ Barner over 2.5 receptions (-138, FanDuel)

Barner has had a relatively quiet start, amassing 12 receptions on 20 targets for 122 yards. He's recorded one touchdown, which came via a goal-line score on a play dubbed "Barnyard" in Seattle.

But while the numbers haven't been overly impressive, I think this matchup against Denver sets up a prime spot for more activity. The Broncos are going to bring copious amounts of pressure, with the hope they can unsettle Darnold. Denver's defense wreaked havoc last weekend in Los Angeles, sacking QB Justin Herbert five times in the victory.

With that in mind, Darnold must get his safety valve(s) involved and I think that puts Barner in a perfect spot to be the benefactor of more targets. He's cleared this number twice in his last three games and will face a defense that has allowed 7.8 targets per game to the tight end position.

Anytime TD scorers

RB Emanuel Wilson (+110, FanDuel)

If we're riding with Wilson on our ladder play and his rushing/receiving prop, you can bet we like him to find the end zone.

Wilson has run for a score in the last two outings, plus he added another touchdown through the air in the Week 4 victory against the Chargers. Coming off a Week 5 effort where he had 22 total touches, I expect that number to climb here and give him several chances to score when Seattle gets deep in Denver territory.

TE Evan Engram (+575, BetMGM)

Engram has put together an eerily similar stats line to the one Barner has produced, hauling in 10 receptions on 18 targets for 121 yards and one touchdown. That lone score came in their season-opening 31-10 loss at the hands of the Kansas City Chiefs.

He had been quiet since that defeat before putting together a solid effort (four catches on four targets for 58 yards) last Sunday. Payton took over the play-calling last week, putting Engram one target behind Jaylen Waddle for team leader.

Now, Denver faces a Seattle defense tied for seveth in the league for sacks (14), meaning Nix — like Darnold – won't have much time in the pocket when facing various blitz packages. And when that happens in the red zone, Engram will be one of first options on Nix's radar.

item.title: NFL Picks Week 6: A Giant Disappointment
item.description: Week 5 proved to be wildly unpredictable. What will Week 6 have in store? Let’s take a look at all of this week’s action to find out.
item.content:encoded:
The New Orleans Saints hit the road to face the New York Giants this week. The Saints are coming off their third-consecutive loss, all at home, no less. Each loss has introduced new levels of shame, sadness, and despair, within the team, the fanbase, and the city. The Saints mean everything to New Orleans, so when they let New Orleans down, it is felt everywhere. A change of scenery for the next few weeks may be what the team and the city needs, as a long road trip east awaits.

To say these Saints and the start to their 2026 season has been a giant disappointment would be a giant understatement. Even team owner Gayle Benson is making statements publicly about the state of the franchise, from the front office, to the coaches, to the players on the field. No one is safe at this point, and no one should be. The Saints will need a giant effort this week to pull off a giant upset on the road. Let’s hope we finally see the spark that lights a fire under this team.

Now let’s take a look at this and all of the matchups in Week 6.

Last week I went 4-11 (YIKES!)

I told you so: 49ers over Seahawks!

What do I know: Titans over Texans?

***

WEEK 6

Thursday, October 15th – Thursday Night Football

Seahawks(3-2) at Broncos(3-2) – Game of the Week

This easily could have been this past February’s Super Bowl matchup, if not for a few bad breaks for Sean Payton’s team, and this game will certainly be better than the Super Bowl we got instead. Expect a defensive slugfest in the Mile High City that ends with a game-winning field goal by Wil Lutz. Denver wins 20-17.

Pick: Broncos

***

Sunday, October 18th – Very Early Game

Texans(1-4) at* Jaguars(4-1) – London, England

Just like last week in London, the Jags win the game late with a field goal that will have the Brits feeling deja-vu. Jacksonville wins 24-23.

Pick: Jaguars

***

Sunday, October 18th – Early Games

Bears(3-2) at Falcons(2-3)

With quarterback injury concerns for both teams, this one will come down to coaching, where Chicago has the distinct advantage. We’ll see if Chicago’s defensive coordinator apologizes to the Falcons for the win, once the game is over. Chicago wins 30-21.

Pick: Bears

***

Ravens(4-1) at Browns(3-2)

Whether Lamar Jackson returns for this AFC North showdown or not, Baltimore will still win a surprisingly one-sided affair on the road, thanks to a monster game from Derrick Henry. Baltimore wins 32-17.

Pick: Ravens

***

Titans(0-5) at Colts(2-3)

Tennessee hit a new low last week, and the lows will continue this week in Indy. Indianapolis wins 39-17.

Pick: Colts

***

Jets(2-3) at Patriots(3-2)

New England will continue to keep pace with Buffalo atop the AFC East while separating from the likes of the Jets. New England wins 35-12.

Pick: Patriots

***

Panthers(2-2) at Eagles(2-3)

Another tough loss for Philly here will definitely have Nick Sirianni on Kellen Moore watch, if he can keep his own head this season. Carolina wins 23-17.

Pick: Panthers

***

Steelers(3-2) at Buccaneers(1-4)

With their eyes towards Paris, the Steelers will be caught flat-footed against the Bucs this week. Tampa Bay wins 24-23.

Pick: Buccaneers

***

Saints(1-4) at Giants(3-1-1)

The way the Saints have played over the past few weeks, this game shouldn’t be close, but the amount of smoke rising from all the hot seats in New Orleans will see the Saints capitalize off turnovers that keep them within striking distance throughout, just not enough to win the game in the end. New York wins 26-23.

Pick: Giants

***

Sunday, October 18th – Late Games

Cardinals(1-4) at Rams(2-3)

Going 2-3 in a brutal five game stretch to start the season has been a disappointment for the Rams, especially losing Monday Night’s heartbreaker, but now they go on a five-game stroll against much easier opponents, bookended by Arizona. The Rams begin their win streak here. Los Angeles wins 42-20.

Pick: Rams

***

Chargers(0-5) at Chiefs(4-0)

If you thought things were brutal in New Orleans, just take a look at Jim Harbaugh’s Chargers, who not only had actual expectations this season, but are failing at those expectations to a spectacular degree. Now they face arguably the best team in the NFL in the most hostile environment in the NFL. We know how this goes. Kansas City wins 35-12.

Pick: Chiefs

***

Bills(4-1) at Raiders(3-2)

After feasting on three of the worst teams in the NFL to start the season, Vegas is now in the middle of a four-game stretch against Super Bowl favorites, and this game won’t go any better for the Raiders than the last two, as the Bills will continue to ride high from their huge win over the Rams last week. Buffalo wins 35-17.

Pick: Bills

***

Sunday Night Football

Cowboys(2-3) at Packers(3-2)

Dallas makes no sense this season. Green Bay makes no sense this season. This game will make no sense either. It will be an offensive explosion at Lambeau, but the Pack will have more offense in this one. Green Bay wins 45-35.

Pick: Packers

***

Monday, October 19th – Monday Night Football

Commanders(1-3-1) at 49ers(5-0)

Washington showed some world-class questionable coaching late in last week’s tie, and that simply won’t cut it against arguably the best-coached franchise in the NFL. This one will be pretty easy for the home team. San Francisco wins 42-14.

***

Pick: 49ers

That’s how I see Week 6 shaping up.  Leave us your picks, comments, and insight below!

item.title: Cardinals Love is not practicing, game status uncertain
item.description: Rookie has another ankle issue
item.content:encoded:
The Arizona Cardinals begin the most difficult portion of their schedule. They will need all of their weapons in each game. This weekend’s contest is against division foe Los Angeles Rams. Both clubs are in dire need of a win.

Cardinals running back Jeremiyah Love is resting his ailing left ankle and has not practiced this week. In fact, it is expected that he won’t see the practice field at all.

RELATED: CARDINALS OFFENSE ONE OF THE MOST BORING

Arizona head coach Mike LaFleur stated that they are dealing with Love’s injury on a daily evaluation. For the ankle to heal completely, obviously, Love will need to stay off it, and the need to see him on the practice field is not a priority.

At a post-practice press conference, LaFleur explained about why Love wasn’t practicing:

“We all are in agreement as much as he wants to battle through, we’re all in agreement right now, it’s just, hey, just give it a little bit of rest and see as the week goes on what that’ll entail for Sunday.”

Right now, his status for the Rams is not known, and could be a game-time decision.

The Cardinals installed a new offense this year based on LaFleur’s past employment with the Rams and San Francisco 49ers’ schemes. Both franchises have very potent offenses, and it is assumed that at some point, Arizona’s will follow suit. But it won’t happen overnight, and the offense will need to have the right components in place. Like an exceptional quarterback and a great, not good, offensive line. Right now, both of these elements are missing.

Love was selected with the third overall pick to supplement this new offense, but so far, he has looked very average. He has played in all five games with four starts. He has rushed for 245 yards on 67 carries, with nine first-down conversions, a single TD, and a pedestrian 3.7 yards per carry average. Love has also been active in the short passing game with 11 catches for 36 yards and another score.

But the expectations were for Love to take the league by storm and become Arizona’s Emmitt Smith or Eric Dickerson. His play hasn’t wowed anyone so far, and he certainly hasn’t hit the big run. He got 90 rushing yards in Week 3 against the San Francisco 49ers on 21 carries. But at no time did he appear ready to hit the big run and take it to the house. In fact, his longest run of the year is nine yards.

And he isn’t the best blocking back since he wasn’t expected to be while at Notre Dame. But that happens quite a bit with rookies, and then they are taught proper techniques.

But Love is a fighter, and isn’t down on his rookie production. LaFleur offered:

“I’m going to try to be as candid as possible with also knowing that everyone’s listening to this, too. He’s a tough dude.” 

Love injured his right ankle against the Las Vegas Raiders in preseason, which kept him out until opening weekend. Technically, it was a high ankle sprain, but it fully healed. Now, he injured his left ankle in the loss to the New York Football Giants, and the injury has lingered, as a lot of ankle issues do.

Fragile ankles at the running back position are not a good thing. Ever.

And for Love, he plays aggressively, especially with his cuts. His explosiveness has been affected since the Giants contest. Is this an issue going forward?

LaFleur added:

“You’d have to ask him that. I know how explosive he is. I know how explosive he wants to be. So, I mean, I think that’s a fair assessment in some aspects. Again, I don’t think it’s an overall hindrance, but again, the rest for him is going to be vital.”

In the event that Love cannot suit up for the LA game, veteran Tyler Allgeier will start and become the bellcow back. Allgeier is in his fifth season and was an important free-agent signing over the offseason. While with Arizona, he has played in all five games with two starts, has gained 119 yards on 35 carries, has six first down conversions, scored once, and has a 3.4 yards-per-carry average. He has great hands and has caught 12 passes for 44 yards.

Bam Knight is healthy and would back up Allgeier. Both are really good blockers when held in. Most likely, the coaching staff would bring up RB Evan Hull from the practice squad against the Rams.

item.title: Texans trade for Pollyanna
item.description: Did Nick Caserio give a 2nd round pick for magic beans and hope?
item.content:encoded:
With an ever present smile, Houston Texans head coach Demeco Ryans ended his latest post-game presser with “Yes, alright, we traded for Marvin Harrison. See ya!”

Dictionary.com

Pollyanna, NOUN

an excessively or blindly optimistic person.

Even when the team is 1-4, with the only win coming against the Tennessee Titans, literally the worst team in pro football, Ryans is smiling. He’s upbeat, joyful, seemingly convinced that no matter how dark the day gets, the sun is rising. All this, despite the current up-ending of the Texans hopes and dreams for 2026, which has left fans in everything but a smiling mood.

Max Barlow over at Casino Gurus, unveiled a new number cruncher for tracking teams dubbed the NFL Pressure Index. In this, we see the following reasons for fans’ frowns to remain upside down

The NFL Pressure Index combines underperformance against preseason expectations (27.8%), recent form (22.2%), painful defeats (15%), playoff pressure (15%), injuries (10%) and performance red flags (10%) to produce a score out of 100.

  • The Texans rank as the NFL’s 7th most pressured team: Scoring 68.8/100 on the NFL Pressure Index. 
  • They have suffered the NFL’s biggest drop in playoff hopes: Their estimated postseason probability has fallen by 33.3%, from 59% to 25%. 
  • Houston is falling short of preseason expectations: The Texans entered the season with a projected win total of 9.5 games, but have started 1-4, 1.8 wins behind their expected total at this stage. 
  • They suffered a particularly painful defeat against Dallas in Week 4: Houston reached an 82% in-game win probability before eventually losing 34-30. 
  • The Texans pressure has however reduced since Week 3: Their score has fallen 17.0 points, from 85.8 to 68.8, moving from 2nd to 7th in the rankings. 

Thankfully, the Texans index score has risen to 68.8, as listed in the last bullet point above. Who currently holds the biggest disappointment? The Los Angeles Chargers roll into the weekend at 89.2/100. At least they have plenty of beaches to enjoy in January.

In trading a 2nd round pick for Marvin Harrison Jr. last weekend, Nick Caserio and the Houston Texans attacked this index. While many people think the price was too steep, word on the street was:

  • The Arizona Cardinals demanded a 2nd round pick for MHJ
  • C.J. Stroud lobbied for Houston to bring MHJ to town
  • The Indianapolis Colts were working to land him

So, giving up a future 2nd round pick to A) land a player your QB wants to play catch with and B) prevent that player from going to your division rival is a win/win on paper. Especially with 1) there’s no guarantee that 2nd round pick was going to bring a player of MHJ’s caliber and 2) Caserio is a horse-trading, card shark who likely will package up something in the off-season to get someone else’s 2nd round pick.

Will the Marvin Harrison Jr. trade fix all that ails the Texans?

Anyone who thinks this team was 1 player away from the Super Bowl hasn’t been paying attention. C.J. Stroud has been balling out, having the best season of his career. And that’s in spite of the abysmal offensive line play, ghosted running game, and head-scratchingly bad defense.

While bringing in MHJ to play catch with his former college QB is certainly a positive on the surface, all the passing yards and receiving touchdowns won’t prevent the defense from giving up last minute game winners to the opposition.

Trading for Derrick Henry might have done more for the team’s fortunes, especially with David Montgomery in the MASH tent. Woody Marks is a quality tailback, but he’s not going to run for 2k behind this poorly coached O-line.

Yet, hope remains.

A lot of people are throwing around the term “bust” when it comes to Marvin Harrison Jr. right now. In his rookie year (2024), Harrison had 16 starts, 116 targets, 62 catches, 885 yards, a 14.3 yard per catch average and 8 touchdowns. All this on the arm of Kyler Murray, who hasn’t exactly been the greatest QB in the league. He did, however, have his 2nd best season when MHJ was a rookie, then fell off soon there after.

While a lot of talking heads are calling MHJ a bust, saying he shouldn’t have been drafted that high, Houston overpaid for him, etc., some people who should know, say things that give Ryans a reason to keep smiling.

This Sunday’s London game in Wembley Stadium against the Jacksonville Jaguars is likely too soon to see a true glimpse into what a Stroud>Nico Collins>Harrison Jr. passing attack looks like. But, don’t be surprised if he makes a statement to show the world the Arizona Cardinals mis-used him.

Will Marvin Harrison Jr. fix all that ails Nick Caley?

In this is where the smile might sink. Harrison was drafted into a poor situation in Phoenix, marginalized, underutilized, and ultimately shelved. How much of this is bad coaching, a poor-scheme fit and a product of the design-the-airplane-in-flight approach to the Cardinals offense over the last several seasons remains to be seen.

It’s easy to believe the narrative, that Harrison has been saved from the bad guys, brought to the good guys, and will now save the day. Especially when watching Ryans light up when he talks about the new wideout.

But we all know the bad coaching existed in Arizona because we’re all too familiar with seeing it here in H-Town. Nick Caley would likely struggle to run a top tier offense in the Big Ten, much less the AFC South. Ben McDaniels (wide receivers/passing game coordinator) and Jerry Shuplinski (QB coach) seem to be the lone bright spots on the Texans offensive coaching staff, however.

And, MHJ will operate largely under their guidance.

Which means, Pollyanna might just thrive in Space City after all.

For those who love to complain: if MHJ does thrive, it might buy Caley more time before the axe eventually falls. A stellar passing game masks the inadequacies of just how bad this offense really is, and Caley benefits most from that masking.

For those who embrace Pollyanna: Winning cures all. And if MHJ can help this team take another AFC South win this weekend, hope will reignite. At this stage, the only real chance this team has of making the playoffs is securing the 4th straight division crown. And in order to do that, they need to run the table, starting this weekend.

#GoTexans! #InDemecoWeTrust

item.title: Panthers vs Eagles: Matchups to watch
item.description: The Carolina Panthers have some intimidating matchups to deal with given some of their injury concerns.
item.content:encoded:
Last time the Carolina Panthers played the Philadelphia Eagles, they were heavy underdogs as a 3-9 team facing an Eagles team that was 10-2 and riding an eight game winning streak. But the Bryce Young-led Panthers were scrappy and hung tight with the Eagles in what was not the most aesthetically pleasing game. Young tried to pull off some heroics, escaping from a possible safety while getting his shirt ripped to complete a pass. He led the Panthers down the field late in a one score game. With less than a minute left, Young hit Xavier Legette with a deep ball to the middle of the field that could have won the game, but Legette let the ball hit the turf. The Panthers ultimately turned the ball over on downs and lost the game.

The lead up to this game is a little different. The Panthers currently have the better record between the two teams, and the vibes around the Eagles especially low for a team that’s 2-3. All time great right tackle suddenly announced his retirement a couple weeks ago, and the Eagles followed that by trading long time starting center Cam Jurgens. And they’ve lost three straight games while all of that has been happening.

The Panthers held up well in their matchups against the Lions, and that allowed them to pull off an electrifying win on Sunday Night Football. Let’s see what this week’s key matchups look like.

Derrick Brown vs Tyler Steen and Markel Bell

The Eagles offensive line has long been one of the strengths of the team, but this season they’re close to recruiting guys off the street to fill in the gaps. Markel Brown has had to fill in after the retirement of Lane Johnson, and he’s no Lane Johnson. Tyler Steen has been okay at right guard, but he got banged up last week and was limited in practice to start the week. Brown has been relatively quiet to start this season. The right side of the Eagles line is where they’re weaker, so it’s a prime spot for Brown to have his best outing of the year and wreck an Eagles offense that has had its fair of struggles.

Devin Lloyd vs Dallas Goedert

Tight end Dallas Goedert led the Eagles in targets against the Jaguars last week with all the injuries to the Eagles best skill position players. With Saquon Barkley and Devonta Smith both questionable this week, there’s a chance Goedert is once again the most established offensive weapon at Jalen Hurts’ disposal. He primarily operates in the short areas of the field. After whatever happened in Week 1, Lloyd has been outstanding in coverage when he’s played. If he can take away Goedert, he’ll take away Hurts’ safety blanket and make a whole lot more difficult for the Eagles offense.

Tetairoa McMillan vs Quinyon Mitchell

McMillan had the game of his life on Sunday Night Football against the Lions. He finished with 14 catches for 192 yards and two touchdowns against a very bad Lions defense. This Sunday’s test is a lot tougher. Quinyon Mitchell has been one of the better corners in the league almost since he arrived in 2024. Jalen Coker is back to help take away some defensive attention, but the Panthers are going to need to trust McMillan to win some one on one matchups against Mitchell to open up things for everyone else.

Robert Hunt vs Jalen Carter

The Eagles defense has been keeping them in games while their offense stumbles around. Jalen Carter is a big part of that. He leads the team with three sacks in five games, which is a very high number for an interior lineman. He’s coming off a dominant performance against the Jaguars in which he was credited with two of those sacks and 1.5 run stuffs. All of the Panthers interior linemen will be responsible for keeping Carter in check, but it’s likely going to be Robert Hunt that handles the bulk of that assignment. Hunt has been a little shaky this season. He’ll need to regain his form from past seasons to limit Carter.

Eagles vs time zones

The Eagles played in London last week, and with the NFL playing so many international games now, that doesn’t always mean a bye in the following week. The London trip certainly seems a lot less daunting now that the NFL forced a couple of teams to play a game in Australia, but it’s still not nothing to travel across six time zones to play a game early in the morning for the body clocks. We’ll see if the Eagles are suffering from any jet lag coming back stateside, especially since they lost the game in heartbreaking fashion before making the long flight home.

item.title: Tyson Bagent Week 5 QB Grade: Bears @ Packers Film Breakdown
item.description: A deeper look with @iamcogs at Tyson Bagent and the Chicago Bears’ deflating 31-7 loss against the Packers.
item.content:encoded:
Well, remember last week when I ended this article by asking which version of Tyson Bagent would show up at Lambeau Field?

We got our answer.

And unfortunately, it was about as bad as it could have been. There was actually quite a bit of optimism surrounding the Bears entering Week 5. Chicago had won three straight games, two of them without Caleb Williams, and Bagent was getting something none of the Bears’ backup quarterbacks had really been afforded yet: a second consecutive start with a full week of preparation knowing the offense was his.

Last week, I came away from the Jets game encouraged by some of the growth Bagent had shown since we last saw him start games in 2023.

He looked more comfortable operating within structure. He was getting through concepts with more confidence, keeping the offense on schedule and, when the pocket stayed clean, was borderline automatic. Against New York, Bagent completed 21 of 23 passes from a clean pocket for 202 yards.

There were warning signs, particularly when pressure arrived and with a handful of turnover-worthy throws, but overall it looked like a more polished version of Tyson Bagent.

Against Green Bay?

Almost all of those encouraging signs disappeared. Bagent completed just 12 of 21 passes for 87 yards, no touchdowns and two interceptions, finishing with a 27.4 passer rating before being benched in favor of Case Keenum. One week after averaging 7.9 yards per attempt against New York, that number cratered to just 4.1 at Lambeau.

And honestly, the box score doesn’t completely capture how difficult the afternoon was.

Green Bay consistently sped Bagent up, forced him off his initial reads and made it difficult for Chicago to find any sort of rhythm offensively. The Bears finished with only 246 yards, averaged 3.6 yards per play and turned the football over five times in a 31-7 loss.

That is about as sharp of a reversal from Week 4 as you’re going to find. Against New York, Bagent generally took what the structure gave him. Against Green Bay, he too often tried to manufacture answers that weren’t there.

His first interception was a good example. After Green Bay opened the game with a touchdown, Chicago had an opportunity to answer, but Bagent tried to force the football to Luther Burden III over the middle. Javon Bullard got underneath the route, deflected the pass and Xavier McKinney came away with the interception.

Green Bay took over in Chicago territory and quickly made it 14-0.

After the game, Bagent acknowledged that he needed to trust his progression and work down to Colston Loveland rather than forcing the ball where he initially wanted to go.

Chicago eventually put together a 16-play touchdown drive late in the second quarter to cut the deficit to 14-7, but that ended up being just about the only sustained offensive success the Bears found all afternoon.

Bagent’s second interception essentially ended any realistic hope of a comeback.

Green Bay initially showed what Bagent believed was a zero blitz before rotating into Cover 2 after the snap. Bagent recognized the change, but not quickly enough, forcing another pass over the middle that McKinney intercepted.

Bagent’s explanation afterward was pretty simple: he was late, and he forced it.

At that point, Ben Johnson had seen enough.

Keenum replaced Bagent after three quarters, with Johnson later saying Bagent never seemed to find a rhythm and that the second interception played a major role in the decision to make a change.

Keenum wasn’t able to rescue the offense either, eventually throwing an interception of his own and losing a fumble as Chicago finished the afternoon with five turnovers.

This certainly wasn’t all on Bagent. The running game that controlled the Jets matchup never got going, while Jordan Love carved up Chicago’s defense for 367 yards and two touchdowns. Green Bay finished with 428 total yards and averaged an absurd 7.3 yards per play.

Nobody wearing a Bears uniform is going to enjoy watching this tape.

But for the purposes of this series, Bagent’s performance is where things get particularly ugly.

Last week, I talked about legitimate signs of development. I thought he looked more comfortable within the offense, more confident in what he was seeing and better equipped to operate within his physical limitations. Sunday was a reminder of just how small the margin for error can be for Bagent.

The accuracy wasn’t consistently there. The processing that looked improved against New York took a major step backward. He forced throws when Green Bay changed the picture, struggled when the defense sped him up and ultimately put the football in danger often enough that Johnson pulled him from the game.

To Bagent’s credit, he didn’t run from it afterward, saying he couldn’t “look any further than the mirror” when evaluating what went wrong.

That’s the response you want from your backup quarterback.

It doesn’t make grading the tape any easier.

I’ve charted plenty of bad quarterback performances since starting this project, but once everything from Sunday was graded and the necessary adjustments were applied, Bagent finished with the lowest adjusted game grade I have ever handed out.

So…This should be fun. Let’s get into the numbers.

Benchmarks

Stat Formatting Key: This week we will be comparing Tyson Bagent’s week 5 start against Williams’ Season Totals and Averages.

(Season totals are underlined, Season Averages in Italics, and this week’s stats appear in regular text.)

C/A:36/55 (65.5%) | 18/27.5 (65.5%) | 12/21 57.1%

Yards:407 | 203.5 | 87

Touchdowns: 4 | 2 | 0

Turnovers: 1| 0.5 | 2

QB at Fault Sacks:0 |0| 2

aDOT:7.7 | 7.1

Passer Rating: 92.0 | 27.1

True Passer Rating:113.4 | 10.1

Time to Throw:3.34s | 3.17s

Time to Pressure:2.75s | 2.86s

Pressure Rate:41.57% | 24.00%

On-Target Rate:83.3% |60.0%

Poor Play Rate / Big Play Rate: 7.5% PPR / 5.0% BRP | 29.6% PPR / 0.0% BRP

EPA per dropback:+0.31 | -0.41

ANY/A:6.2 | -0.9

Game Scorecard

The full grading sheet for each play can be found here.

Game Notes

Note: Last year, I included PFF grades in these breakdowns. With PFF continuing to expand its use of AI across its platform, and with my confidence in how accurately its grades reflect quarterback performance declining, I’ve decided to move away from them this season. In their place, I’ll be using PFN’s Impact Score, which will be notated as PFN on grading sheets moving forward.

NFL Passer Rating / True Passer Rating / PFN Impact Score: 27.4 / 10.1 / 65.9

  • The NFL’s average passer rating through Week 4 sat at 92.2. For some added perspective, if Bagent simply threw every pass harmlessly incomplete without an interception, his passer rating would still be 39.6. His actual mark was 27.4. So, yeah… not great.
  • A 10.1 TPR is an absolute disaster of a start.
    • A lot has to go wrong to post a TPR this low. Bagent was inefficient over a decent-sized sample, took two sacks, threw two interceptions and generated almost nothing downfield. By my charting, he completed just one pass more than 10 yards downfield. All of that converged into a 10.1 TPR, the lowest mark I’ve recorded in any QB start I’ve graded.
  • On the PFN scale, where 75 represents an average qualifying starter and 90 is elite territory, Bagent finished Week 5 with a 65.9 Impact Score, ranking 24th of 30 qualifying quarterbacks.
    • The underlying numbers fell off a cliff as well. His EPA/dropback dropped from +0.22 in Week 4 to -0.41, while his CPOE fell nearly 20 percentage points, from +8.0% to -10.9%. His Week 5 EPA/dropback ranked 26th, while his CPOE ranked 28th of 30 qualifiers.
    • His success rate also fell from 61.1% in Week 4 to 40.0% against the Packers.

On-Target Throws: 2026 Average: 83.3% | Week 5: 60.0%

  • Reminder: Completion percentage ≠ On-Target Percentage. I only chart aimed passes, meaning throwaways, spikes and passes deflected at the line are excluded. Drops can still be credited as on-target.
  • Short-Level Passing (Behind LOS–9 yards): 11/15 | 73.3% On-Target
  • Deep-Level Passing (10+ Yards Downfield): 1/5 | 20.0% On-Target
    • Bagent’s inability to push the ball downfield made Green Bay’s job considerably easier. He attempted just five passes more than 10 yards downfield, completing one, while two ended up in Packers hands.
    • Green Bay was able to focus on taking away the run and underneath game while daring Bagent to beat them farther downfield. He simply couldn’t do it.

Poor Play Rate / Big Play Rate: 29.6% PPR / 0.0% BPR

  • Last week I said an 11.6% Poor Play Rate was less than ideal. A 29.6% rate is borderline criminal.
  • Bagent recorded two turnover-worthy throws, giving him five across his two starts, while the negative grades continued piling up elsewhere.
  • The biggest difference from Week 4? A 0.0% Big Play Rate. Bagent recorded just two plays graded above “Average,” with his best mark coming on a “Good” throw to Rome Odunze for 17 yards early in the third quarter.
  • There wasn’t a single “Great” or “Elite” play to offset the mistakes.

EPA per Dropback: -0.41

  • Another massive reversal from Week 4, when Bagent ranked 11th among qualifying quarterbacks at +0.22 EPA/dropback. His -0.41 mark against Green Bay fell to 26th of 30 qualifiers.
  • Two interceptions and a pair of costly sacks loomed large, and there simply weren’t enough positive plays to dig the offense out of that hole.

Under Pressure: 24.0%

  • By my charting, Bagent was pressured on 24.0% of his dropbacks. The Bears’ offensive line wasn’t as dominant as it was against New York, but that still isn’t an overwhelming amount of pressure for a quarterback to deal with.
  • Pair that with a Time to Throw north of three seconds, and you would hope Bagent could take advantage of the time he was afforded. Instead, the accuracy and processing issues persisted even when Green Bay wasn’t immediately disrupting the pocket.
  • That tracks with the broader film evaluation. NFL.com noted Bagent struggled to diagnose coverages and became increasingly skittish in the pocket before Chicago eventually turned to Case Keenum.

From Here to Infamy

  • To date, I’ve graded more than 200 NFL quarterback performances. I’ve seen some dizzying highs and some absolutely cratering lows, but Bagent’s -10.20 adjusted game score is the lowest I’ve ever handed out. As a reminder, graded games get an adjusted score if they fall under 39 total plays to grade, by taking the average points per play (amount of graded points earned totaled and divided by total plays graded) we multiply that number by however many plays we need to get to 39. In Tyson’s case that was -0.2625 graded points per play.
  • Even without the adjustments, his raw game score of -7.05 would still rank among the bottom five performances I’ve graded.
  • And he managed to do all of that in just 27 graded snaps.

Play Reviews

This week I’m doing something different, I want to highlight a few examples of things that (in my opinion) Tyson missed out on, whether that be due to blinders, purposefully moving past a receiver, or misdiagnosis of a defense is up to the individual, but the tape was rife with Bears receivers open, with Tyson seemingly missing them, or throwing to someone who clearly was not open.

Play 1: Tyson escapes the pocket and has Luther Burden III working with him towards the left sideline with no defender within 5 yards, if Tyson hits his man here it’s an easy chunk play and with Burden’s YAC ability maybe even a score, Bagent instead scrambles for 4-yards on the play.

Play 2: Another play with Bagent rolling to his right this time he has Kalif Raymond breaking open with a defender trailer, an accurate throw to Raymond gives him a chance to turn up field and do some real damage, Tyson does pick up 6 yards on the scramble which constitutes a successful run, but one wonders the meat left on bone.

Play 3: We have a clean pocket on this play with Bagent scanning the middle of the field, a throw with anticipation as Raymond is making his break gives him a legitimate shot at scoring, but Bagent hesitates then breaks out of the pocket leading to this. Fortunately the Packers were called for a hold leading to a first down.

Play 4: This is another simple one where Bagent bypasses an easy completion due to hesitation, it’s a simple hitch route, throwing it with a small amount of anticipation should lead to an easy 6-yards. Instead Bagents moves on, scrambles out of the pocket, slips and takes a sack.

Play 5: Bagent starts this rep working the corner route to Loveland, the window is there with proper anticipation and ball placement, however he quickly moves off that, and begins to stare down the checkdown to Kmet, despite the backside dig from Burden coming open. This ends up as an incompletion due to an inaccurate throw to Kmet on the checkdown.

Play 6: Interception #1, the dig is well covered, the underneath defender has depth on the route taking away any throwing window. Instead of checking the ball down to an open Loveland, Tyson forces a ball into a non-existent window, and the Packers come away with a turnover.

Play 7: Burden and Rome are running a Cross concept from the top of the screen, with some anticipation and touch Bagent should be able to get the ball over the intermediate defenders allowing Burden to do his YAC thing, instead Bagent checks the ball down to Raymond for 3 yards.

Play 8: Probably the most egregious miss by Bagent, the Packers fail in passing off Burder as he runs a shallow crossing route, Bagent is literally all eyes on Burden, but does not pull the trigger. With Burden’s after the catch ability this has a chance for a touchdown, instead it ends with Bagent wrapped up by a Packers defender for a sack.

Play 9: Bagent has a clean pocket here, targeting Loveland with an shallow dig. The Packers have numbers on the left side and drop into zone coverage meaning every key defender on the left side can react to Bagent throwing. Instead of working the play to the backside with Raymond, Bagent forces the ball into impossible coverage, and is lucky the ball sails past defenders harmlessly.

Summary

Bagent finishes Week 5 with final grades of 1st Half (-4.50) / 2nd Half (-2.55) / Game (-10.20) (adjusted score), equating to a truly “Awful” game grade.

There really isn’t much of a positive spin to put on this one.

One week after I came away encouraged by some of the growth Bagent showed against the Jets, nearly everything went in the opposite direction at Lambeau. The accuracy cratered, the processing became increasingly shaky when Green Bay changed the picture after the snap, and the turnover-worthy decisions piled up without enough positive plays to offset them.

The result was the lowest adjusted game score I’ve handed out in more than 200 quarterback performances.

Of the quarterbacks I’m grading this season, you can see where Bagent’s Week 5 score landed him, 6th of 6 players graded in Week 4. For a look at the entire season thus far, along with some quick notes on the other quarterbacks from this week, you can find that here.

This wasn’t simply one or two disastrous plays sinking an otherwise competent afternoon. Bagent finished with a 29.6% Poor Play Rate, failed to record a single Big Play and produced just two snaps that I graded above “Average.” Even his unadjusted score would still land among the five worst performances I’ve graded.

Twenty-seven graded snaps were enough to reach some pretty remarkable depths.

That’s especially disappointing after Week 4. Against New York, Bagent showed legitimate signs that he had developed from the quarterback we saw starting games in 2023. I don’t think one afternoon completely erases that progress, but Green Bay provided a pretty harsh reminder of the limitations that can surface when the offense needs Bagent to consistently make plays beyond its structure.

Eventually, Ben Johnson had seen enough too, turning to Case Keenum for the fourth quarter.

Thankfully for the Bears, there may finally be some light at the end of this weird three-week quarterback tunnel.

Caleb Williams took his biggest step toward returning Wednesday, when the Bears listed him as a full participant for the first time since the hamstring injury he suffered against Minnesota in Week 2. Johnson is still keeping his cards close to the vest, calling the quarterback situation “fluid,” but this is easily the most encouraging update we’ve received since Williams went down. The Bears have more on Williams’ progress here.

After watching Keenum and Bagent combine to keep the Bears afloat for a couple of weeks, followed by everything completely unraveling in Green Bay, the possibility of getting Williams back against Atlanta couldn’t come at a much better time.

We’ll see if he’s ready to go.

Until then, Bear Down!

Gary Baugher Jr. is a second year contributor to WCG, bringing football insight backed by over 16 years of experience in organized football and more than 30 years as a passionate fan of the game. You can follow him on Twitter at @iamcogs.

item.title: Scouting Report: California Golden Bears
item.description: A quick look at the Golden Bears
item.content:encoded:
The Basics

Team: California Golden Bears

Location: Berkley, California

Enrollment: 33,000

Head Coach: Tosh Lupoi (3-3)

Record: 3-3

Wins: Syracuse, Wagner, VT

Losses: UCLA, Clemson, UNLV

Recruiting Rank: 50 (2 4-stars, 16 3-stars)

Transfer Portal Rank: 14 (7 4-stars, 23 3-stars)

Win Total: 5.5

Spread: Wake -9.5

The Deacs have entered the top 25 for the first time in 4 years, but to stay there, they are going to have to beat California on the entire opposite side of the country. Traveling to the west coast sounds like a bigger obstacle than it is—in 3 years of ACC play, California and Stanford are just a combined 7-11 in conference play against teams making the journey west. There is evidence that the west coast trip has a bigger negative impact on a team’s next game, but the Deacs are on bye, so that really shouldn’t bother them at all.

Offense

Points per game: 26.7 (86th out of 138)

Yards per game: 397.2 (68th)

Run/pass: 40% run, 60% pass

Rush yards per game: 92.8 (134)

Pass yards per game: 304.3 (14)

3rd down conversions: 38% (89)

Sacks allowedper game: 1.8 (75)

Turnovers: 8 (81)

The first thing that jumps out to me about the Cal offense is just how much they throw the ball—Cal is 1 of 8 teams in the nation throwing the ball on over 55% of their plays, and only Hawaii attempts more passes per game than the Golden Bears. Even with backup quarterback Jackson Brousseau in last week against VT, Cal threw the ball 43 times for 321 yards.

I imagine a big part of that is simply that the Golden Bears haven’t been successful running the ball at all this season. With last season’s leading rusher Kendrick Raphael now at SMU, the Golden Bears are managing a meager 3.3 yards per carry on the ground, good for 123rd in the nation. Outside of their game against FCS Wagner, Cal has run for 100+ yards 1 time this season (UCLA) and has not surpassed 3.2 yards per carry in a single game. The Wake Forest defense just held the Wolfpack to 15 total rushing yards on 24 carries (0.6 avg) last weekend, so they should have no trouble slowing down a less than stellar Cal rushing attack.

The other reason to throw the ball that much is having a QB like Jaron-Keawe Sagapolutele (JKS). After his freshman season at Cal, where he threw for 3,454 yards and 18 touchdowns, JKS entered the 2026 season as one of the most hyped quarterbacks in the country.

Despite that, he has had a pretty slow start to the season this year. In his 4 FBS games in 2026, JKS is completing 61% of his passes for just 767 yards, 5 touchdowns, and 5 interceptions. The left hander still has a massive arm capable of throwing frozen ropes 50 yards down the field, but it seems like he may be experiencing a bit of a sophomore slump. It doesn’t help that the Bears started the season with a 30 year old offensive coordinator with 0 play-calling experience, who was recently replaced at halftime of the UNLV game after the Golden Bears fell behind 24-7.

After making the switch, the Golden Bears scored 24 second half points against UNLV and put up 400 yards of offense and 25 points with a backup quarterback to beat 4-1 Virginia Tech last week. Wake fans should know the impact the the right offensive coordinator can have on quarterback play watching Gio Lopez this season, so as JKS likely returns from a concussion this week to take on the Deacs, Wake should be prepared for him to look much more like the freshman phenom of last year with McCann calling the plays.

A team that throws the ball over 40 times per game is obviously going to need some good receivers. Unlike the Deacs, who have 1 receiver with almost more catches than the rest of the wide receivers on the team combined, Cal spreads the ball around a lot more. The Golden Bears have 6 players with 10+ receptions and 9 different players with at least 1 touchdown catch so far this season. Ohio transfer Chase Hendricks (39 catches, 361 yards, 2 TD) and Rutgers transfer Ian Strong (28 catches, 396 yards, 1 TD) are the two most targeted players, but tight ends and running backs are also integral in the Cal passing attack—backs have caught a combined 32 passes for 318 yards and 3 touchdowns this season, while tight ends have added 26 catches for 329 yards and 2 touchdowns.

Defense

Points allowed per game: 25.5 (85)

Yards allowed per game: 367.5 (86)

Rush yards allowed per game: 175.0 (109)

Pass yards allowed per game: 192.5 (47)

3rd down defense: 40% (94)

Sacks per game: 2.17 (60)

Turnovers Forced: 9 (25)

Defense has been the stronger unit for the Bears this season, which makes sense considering Cal has a former defensive lineman as a head coach and former NFL linebacker Ron Rivera as a GM. Most of the strength of the defense lies in the secondary—Cal is currently 10th in the nation in EPA/play on passing plays, and they have only allowed over 200 passing yards in 2 of their 6 games this season. A big part of that was Cal’s focus in the transfer portal this offseason. The Golden Bears brought in 5 defensive backs in the portal, including Kingston Lopa from Oregon, Daniel Harris from Georgia, Ricky Fletch from Ole Miss, and Marquis Groves-Killebrew from Arizona. Lopa is currently leading the nation with 5 interceptions this season and is the highest graded safety in the ACC per PFN.

With his ability in coverage and run support at 6-5, 200 pounds, I don’t see how Lopa is not an early round NFL draft pick next summer. He did miss Cal’s last game with a concussion, so whether or not he is good to go on Saturday will likely significantly change the Wake’s ability to throw the ball down the field.

While the pass defense has been exceptional for Cal, the run defense has left a lot to be desired—the Golden Bears are currently 127th in the nation in EPA/rush and are giving up 4.9 yards per rush (118th). Again, the transfer portal may be a main culprit here. Cal lost both of their starting linebackers—1st Team All-ACC selection Cade Uluave (BYU) and Luke Ferrelli (Ole Miss)—from last season, and that duo combined for 191 tackles, 17 tackles for loss, and 4 sacks last season. USC transfer AJ Tuitele (33 tackles, 4 TFL, 3 sacks) has done a solid job trying to fill the void, but he was ejected for targeting in the 4th quarter of the Virginia Tech game—since that was his 2nd targeting ejection of the season, he should be out for the first half of the Wake game.

Another guy that could give Wake some trouble establishing the run is Oregon transfer Jericho Johnson. At 6-4, 345 pounds, Johnson is tough man to block and is currently 2nd on the team with 3.5 tackles for loss this season.

The Deacs have not been great on the ground this season, averaging just 144 rushing yards per game and 4.2 yards per carry this. Hopefully Wake can find a way to get the rushing attack going against the Golden Bears, because when Cal allows over 150 yards on the ground, they are 0-3 (UCLA, UNLV, Clemson). When they hold their opponent to below 150 yards rushing, they are a perfect 3-0 (Syracuse, Wagner, VT).

One final note on this matchup: expect a lot of flags. California is the first team Wake will play that currently averages more penalties and penalty yards than the Deacs this season. Wake is 10th in the nation in penalties and 7th in yardage, averaging 8.7 penalties for 79.8 yards per game. The Golden Bears are 4th and 2nd in the same categories respectively, averaging 9.5 penalties for 89.7 yards per game. Wake has only had fewer penalty yards than their opponent 1 time this season (against Louisville by 5 whole yards), so it would be nice to do that again.

I think Wake has proven to be the better team so far this season, but Cal appears to be improving with the shakeup to the coaching staff. Assistant Head Coach Nick Rolovich gave Jake Dickert his first Power 5 job when he hired him as the defensive coordinator at Washington State in 2020, so he could have some trade secrets on how to stop the man who eventually took his job in 2021. Hopefully the Deacs can survive the west coast trip and get to the bye week with a win.

Go Deacs!

item.title: Chiefs Market Movers: Who’s trending up or down out of the bye
item.description: Whose stock is up and whose is down among Kansas City’s roster in Week 6?
item.content:encoded:
It’s been an interesting season so far—with the early bye week, it’s not quite a mid-season review, but it’s a great time to check in on some of the trends we’ve seen over the first four weeks.

Your 4-0 Kansas City Chiefs are playing good defense and running the ball like it’s 1997. They have an OPOY candidate (running back Kenneth Walker) and an MVP (quarterback Patrick Mahomes). The rookies are playing well, and the coaching staff changes seem to have helped.

On the other hand, injuries, penalties, and pass-rush and pass-protection issues have been frustrating, and a couple of their wins were closer than they should be.

Here are a few Chiefs who seem to be trending up or down.

BULLS 

Running back Kenneth Walker III: The offseason narrative: Kansas City made only one significant offensive addition, and he’s a running back. The reality: it’s changed everything. Walker is leading the league in nearly every statistical category. He’s already racked up big plays of 60 and 76 yards, and has been on the field for three-fourths of the offensive snaps so far. The coaching staff has committed to a new-old-style offense with plenty of under-center handoffs, screens, and play-action passes. They found the perfect guy to execute on the field, and it’s paying off. The only question left is whether they can do this in January and February.

Cornerbacks Mansoor Delane and Nohl Williams: If the trend continues, we may have to talk about these guys every week. They’ve both shown the skill set and makeup to be an elite tandem in this league. Barring injury, my only concern is that the coaching staff tries moving one of them inside because of shortcomings there (see Bears below). Otherwise, these two are making Andy Reid, Steve Spagnuolo, and Brett Veach look very smart for letting those other guys walk.

Offensive lineman Kahlil Benson: Going back to the premise of this series, we’re looking for those who are trending in one way or another, even if they aren’t the top-of-the-roster guys. Just think back to the expectations we had for a player, and how they have over (or under) performed compared to those expectations— or compared to their contract/draft slot.

Given that context, it seems logical that we should be extremely bullish on Kahlil Benson. The guy wasn’t even considered a priority UDFA; he had to earn his roster spot via tryout and a strong offseason. Even then, there was lots of panic and doubt when he struggled in a couple of preseason games. He earned the starting nod and has more than held his own. Yes, the coaching staff is giving him more help than they normally allow a tackle, but by any measure Benson has performed well in the role he was asked to fill. As the season wears on, they’ll need him— whether he’s the starting left tackle, starting at another spot, or as depth—he is part of the solution.

Others trending in the right direction this week: Emmet Johnson, George Karlaftis, Travis Kelce, Drue Tranquill, Kristian Fulton, Matt Araiza, Xavier Nwankpa, Felix Anudike-Uzomah

BEARS

Defensive tackle Chris Jones: It’s weird putting Chris on this list. He’s an elite player in this league, and will belong in the Hall of Fame. He’s made a fantastic living terrorizing quarterbacks from the interior of the defensive line. He’s been unblockable in key situations. But this season, he’s clearly fighting through injury and simply hasn’t been as disruptive as we’re used to. Jones doesn’t have a single sack yet this season, despite playing primarily in pass-rushing situations. Part of the issue could be his usage—the team has aligned him outside on most snaps. Chris Jones can do that—occasionally. But his bread and butter is destroying guards and double-teams on the inside. Maybe they’re trying to save him some wear and tear for later in the season?

The entire Slot/Nickel Cornerback position group: It seemed obvious the Chiefs wanted to address this position coming into 2026, and they did, throwing a bunch of options out there. They drafted Jadon Canaday, signed Kader Kohu, brought L’Jarius Sneed back, and retained Chris Roland-Wallace and (gulp) Chamarri Conner. Sneed has been the guy thus far, playing 76% of the team’s defensive snaps at the position. The results have been predictably mixed— Sneed has been involved in some significant plays, including the forced-and-recovered fumble against the Dolphins. But teams have found lots of success with quick passes against Sneed. It’s one of those things that can wreck a pass defense— when QBs have a quick/easy option to complete a pass on one guy, it neutralizes a good pass rush.

Fullback Khyiris Tonga: For a minute there, it looked like the Chiefs could dominate on third-and-fourth-and-1, but forward progress seems to have stalled over the last two games. Using defensive tackle Khyiris Tonga at fullback was a fun changeup, but teams seem to have completely caught on. Hopefully, Andy Reid was just setting up some future looks by handing the ball to Tonga a couple of times. They need to move the sticks better in these situations, and using an actual fullback may be part of the answer.

Others trending in the wrong direction this week: Jack Cochrane, Rashee Rice, Kingsley Suamataia, Mike Caliendo

VALUE (SLEEPER) PICKS:

Defensive lineman Omarr Norman-Lott: ONL may be the forgotten man on this defensive front, but he may be close to returning and reminding folks why they missed him. A quick, stout interior defensive lineman who can rotate in on the pass rush, Norman-Lott can absolutely help.

Left Tackle Josh Simmons: The fickle nature of NFL fans, media, social media, and other commentators is insane. Josh Simmons was the left tackle that we’ve always wanted in Kansas City. But then he missed the first four games with a back injury, and sentiment around Simmons plummeted—even faster than sentiment around the Chargers. Well, Simmons is back at practice after the bye week, and I’m sure many who have been sleeping on him will jump back on the bandwagon once he’s in the lineup. From what we know, he didn’t stop caring, and he didn’t forget how to play football. There’s a non-zero chance we’ll forget the Simmons criticism by the end of the postseason.

Linebacker Jeffrey Bassa: It feels like an annual tradition with these Chiefs: acquire an athletic linebacker, bury him on the depth chart behind some one-dimensional coaches’ favorites. Then, we all complain that Spagnuolo needs a guy like that on the field. Why aren’t they playing this guy? Is this another case of a guy who “doesn’t understand the playbook?” If so, could the playbook be the real problem? Bassa appears to be that guy this season. Yes, it’s early, but (as mentioned above) Chiefs opponents have been picking on defenders with quick passes over the middle. Bassa is only a few games into his rookie season, but it’s time to give him a shot. He can be a playmaker— unless there’s something we don’t understand (there often is).

item.title: Nick Sirianni’s Eagles career is at a crossroads
item.description: Will Sunday be the beginning of the end of an era, or the launchpad back to respectability?
item.content:encoded:
As the days have passed following last Sunday’s nightmare-fueled loss to Jacksonville in London, and all angles of Nick Sirianni’s last minute decision to allow the Jaguars an opportunity to return the final kickoff have been dissected to within an inch of its life (including by me), I think it’s fair to say this week’s home game against the Carolina Panthers is a crossroads for the embattled head coach.

Upon further reflection, I can agree that his kickoff decision last week can be argued both ways. There were sound reasons to kick it through the end zone (still is the right call in my opinion) and to allow a return. There are other aspects of those final moments that deserve scrutiny, specifically whether Jalen Hurts, Makai Lemon, and Sean Mannion executed those final seconds correctly. But in the end, it was virtually impossible for the Jaguars to win a game with eight seconds left, no timeouts and about to receive a kickoff.

In 999 times out of 1000, the Eagles win with no issues and none of those decisions are discussed. Ever.

Perhaps the greater point of emphasis on the job Sirianni did last Sunday should be on the team’s overall performance.

Coming off back-to-back losses and fielding a wildly undermanned roster, Sirianni had his team up for that game in London. They flew across the ocean, knowing they had less talent on the field than their opponent, and should have won a game in which they were massive underdogs. That Sirianni was able to coax that kind of effort out of a pedestrian roster last Sunday is a testament to his ability to get his players to play hard for him.

That’s why Sunday’s game against Carolina is such an important one for him, and the organization.

We’ve seen the head coaching life cycle under Jeffrey Lurie. When things start to go bad, the front office doesn’t let situations linger. They make quick decisions.

Andy Reid was dismissed after a 4-12 season in 2012 that was preceded by an 8-8 season the year before. Doug Pederson was let go after just one losing season, a 4-11-1 campaign during the COVID year of 2020. When Lurie and Howie Roseman feel a coach’s life cycle has come and gone, they act quickly. The 2012 and ‘20 seasons spun wildly out of control on both coaches to the point a change became inevitable.

A win on Sunday stops the bleeding and at least signals this year may not spiral out of control. It’s similar to Week 6 of the 2024 Super Bowl season. Coming off a ‘23 campaign in which the team fell apart and collapsed in spectacular fashion, the Eagles started 2-2 and coming off a humiliating loss to the Bucs in Tampa. There was a very real feeling that if Sirianni didn’t take care of business coming out of that bye week, he might be fired in-season.

It wasn’t pretty, but with a new run-first, no-turnover offensive philosophy and a defense that was finding its legs, the Eagles edged the Browns 20-16 in an ugly home win. But, it was a victory that launched a 10-game winning streak. They would lose just one more time the entire season before winning it all.

That won’t happen this time. There won’t be any 10-game winning streaks, and the likelihood of this team winning a Super Bowl at this moment is exceedingly remote. No one is expecting that right now, but a loss and, more to the point, a lackluster effort at the Linc, could spell doom for the future of Sirianni as head coach of the Eagles. There is no chance anyone is fired in the middle of the season, but how this team plays down the stretch will determine whether Sirianni has a long-term future in Philadelphia.

And make no mistake, Sirianni will attempt on Sunday to do something no NFL team has ever successfully done — win a game in which a team is coming off an international game and has to play a team coming off a bye week. It’s only happened four times before, and teams in the Birds’ position are 0-4. This was the Eagles’ choice, by the way. They could have scheduled their bye week coming back from London, but chose to push it later in the season. Nevertheless, it would be a remarkable thing if Sirianni has this team up and running at full capacity on Sunday afternoon against a team coming off a two-week break.

It’s fair to wonder if Sirianni lost the locker room last Sunday, even if his decision to allow a return was defensible. He has taken full responsibility for last week’s debacle, a noble act. And while that is certainly appreciated by his players, and while his players all want to do well for him, how will they respond to that? Do they see their boss taking ownership of a questionable decision and continue to rally behind him? Or do they see him as a good guy that lacks answers on how to fix a lackluster offense and has had an uneven track record of making in-game decisions?

In short, do the players trust him?

If they do, you will see an Eagles team come out of the locker room on Sunday ready, once again, to play hard. Despite being the home team, it is essentially a pick ‘em game, meaning most oddsmakers believe Carolina is the better team. But it was clear last week that Jacksonville was the better team by a significant margin, and the Birds almost shocked the world by stealing a game in which they were touchdown-underdogs.

Sirianni and the Eagles are paying the price for winning a Super Bowl two seasons ago. Two of their offensive linemen essentially broke themselves doing it, and they’ve never recovered. Their veteran offensive coordinator left to take another job, and they’ve struggled to replace him ever since. Their star wide receiver revealed team goals weren’t as important to him following the Super Bowl and played his way out of town in pursuit of singular glory. And the litany of injuries they’ve suffered, along with the sudden retirement of Lane Johnson, has almost forced the ushering of a new era upon the franchise before they were ready for it.

About the only thing that hasn’t happened is an injury to their star quarterback, which I hope I haven’t now spoken into existence. And let’s not pretend there isn’t uncertainty over whether Jalen Hurts can truly ever be successful in an offense that asks him to play a style of football he never has before and has never appeared comfortable playing.

It’s almost impossible to quickly return to a Super Bowl without a ton of luck on your side, and the Eagles have had none of it this year. That’s OK. That happens. This has been an unbelievable run, and Sirianni has had remarkable injury luck over his first five seasons. But that bill is coming due now.

The Eagles may finish with a record under .500. Coaches can survive that as long as progress can be seen on the field and the product is not embarrassing. Good coaches help less talented teams play over their heads and improve as the season moves along. There are not a ton of healthy Pro Bowlers left on the roster, so every player on the team needs to be coached up even more now. It is imperative this coaching staff, specifically on the offensive side of the ball, gives this team an edge.

The Eagles must play smarter football than the guys lined up against them. They cannot rely on their talent to paper over execution problems and mistakes. They cannot be a heavily-penalized team. They cannot make bad decisions. Virtually every in-game decision has to have the correct process, even if the results don’t go their way.

If they play smart, competent football, Sirianni should keep his job, no matter the record. He’s a CEO head coach, and must be the very best version of that for this project to work. This Sunday begins an opportunity to show he can get the most out of his talent and defy the critics who believe his coordinators and Howie Roseman’s roster have carried him to two Super Bowls. He needs to be a force multiplier, a positive agent for success.

He needs to give the Eagles an edge.

This Sunday against Carolina will give us a pretty good indication how the team feels about its head coach, which will go a long way in determining how the front office should feel about him, too.

item.title: Los Angeles Chargers news: Should the Bolts rush anyone back before the bye?
item.description: Should the Chargers avoid rushing back any players to face the Chiefs ahead of their Week 7 bye?
item.content:encoded:
The Chargers opened Week Six with a whopping 18 players on their Wednesday injury report (veteran Khalil Mack not included) which was a new season-high for players on any given report thus far.

In an almost surreal situation, the Chargers ended Sunday’s loss to the Broncos with three healthy wide receivers who were dressed (Derius Davis, MVS, and Theo Wease) on top of four rookie offensive linemen who were forced to start due to six other injuries to players ahead of them on the depth chart.

The team is 0-5 and have a date with the 5-0 Chiefs this week.

Is it even worth the risk to try and have players such as Ladd McConkey, Derwin James, and Donte Jackson return just before the team’s bye? There’s a number of other players who could also make a return this week from various injuries, but again, what’s the point?

It would almost be more beneficial for the young guns to go out there again and face a very good team to further understand the talent level at the top of the league. Trial by fire isn’t always a bad thing!

item.title: Fantasy Football Start 'Em, Sit 'Em: Need help for the flex spot in Week 6? Joel Smyth has lineup advice
item.description: Fantasy football analyst Joel Smyth examines the flex options out in a bye-heavy Week 6.
item.content:encoded:
We're on to Week 6 of the fantasy season! As we look for every advantage this season, the X-factor position is the FLEX. To break it all down, analyst Joel Smyth goes through 8 players in the consensus rankings flex zone for your flexes, double flexes or even third WR slots.​

​Set & Forget​

Braelon Allen vs. NE

After his second straight game as the Jets bellcow, this time getting 28 opportunities, I'm not considering moving Allen out of the lineup. If this game goes how New York wants, Allen can cross 20 carries once more with the Jets controlling this matchup.

Say it doesn't. Well, Allen was second among RBs last week in route share to Christian McCaffrey. His four targets only equaled one zero-yard reception, but it does provide a little bit of a buffer in future games as the lead back.

Jalen Coker vs. PHI​

An insane split to start the season: Philadelphia is No. 1 against outside WRs, and 32nd versus the slot, where Jalen Coker lines up close to half of plays. With a lot of star wideouts on bye, Coker becomes a set-it-and-forget-it player upon his return for me. In his previous three healthy games, Coker had 8+ receptions in all of them!

The bye week came at a perfect time for a player who was close to being ready to go after another week of rest.

Flex Starts

Denzel Boston vs. BAL

Boston is getting the high-value targets in Cleveland, ranking 10th in air yards on the season as the clear top option on downfield throws. His average depth of target is 16 yards downfield, making him a more boom-or-bust flex, but without KC Concepcion, he should be the main focus of this passing attack. With five end-zone targets so far this season (behind only Christian Watson), the touchdown upside is higher than one would expect on a Browns offense. Hopefully, head coach Todd Monken can learn from all his practices versus Baltimore's defense over the last few years and exploit them for a few big plays.

Devaughn Vele vs. NYG

It's hindsight, but Vele's down week was pretty predictable, right? Minnesota's defense is insane and shouldn't be the matchup to dissect negatively too much. Tyler Shough was held to 96 passing yards after having 250+ in all four games prior, as the Vikings held the Saints to 13 points. Vele's volume has been anywhere from 6-9 targets in each game, supported by a very fantasy-friendly offense for PPR leagues. New Orleans plays ultra-fast, takes the easy completions, is pass-heavy and often trailing. In his first month against non-Vikings defenses, Vele averaged 13.9 PPR PPG. I'd expect production more similar to that versus the Giants in Week 6.

Double Flex Starts

Dameon Pierce vs. CAR​

It's not a plug-and-play, but more so a plug-and-pray. The RB position is thinning fast, and four bye weeks don't help. A lot of teams just need a body at RB and Pierce's body is out there every play! That's the main positive — after the Will Shipley injury, Pierce played every snap for the Eagles.

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Basketball league for the 2026-27 NBA season

Is the offensive line in front of him good? Not really. Also, neither is the offense. And probably not Pierce himself. However, he's going to get touches, and in fantasy, sometimes that's enough. It's worked for Ollie Gordon II, at times for MarShawn Lloyd and several others in bad situations in spot starts.

Jeremiyah Love vs. LAR

In comparison to the other double-flex options, I like Love's odds the best. He's been a disappointing third-round fantasy pick to say the least, but his ceiling is still the best of the players in this area. Before the blowout, Love handled 90% of the Cardinals' RB carries, continuing a trend over the last month.

The floor is low against a great Rams squad, but it's not any lower than the replacements, and at least gives you a shot at a very talented player getting a good amount of touches in this divisional matchup. The goal would be to get the outcome we saw versus a good 49ers team, where Love had 26 touches and reached the end zone. Since that point, he's had over 70% of the RB touches.

Booby Traps

Harold Fannin Jr. vs. BAL

I'd rather be playing Boston than trusting in a Fannin bounce back. The injury to KC Concepcion does help him in theory, although it didn't help much for Fannin's Week 5 production; it isn't enough for me to place him in lineups. The role is minimal to begin the season. He has zero designed targets and relies too much on checkdowns from Deshaun Watson, who has the most scramble attempts in the NFL. Fannin has three touchdowns, but they've come on only three red-zone targets, an unsustainable rate. With his target share all over the place, I'm not banking on it to be above 20% for just the second time this year.

Rome Odunze vs. ATL

I'm an Odunze apologist, and I hope he can bounce back with Caleb Williams; I just don't think this is his best spot. Williams really struggled under pressure last season when it came to his passing. When he was under pressure, Odunze had an abysmal 0.58 yards per route, being targeted once in a blue moon. I bring this up specifically because Atlanta, which has lost key edge rushers, has overcome the odds to lead the league in pressure rate this season. It doesn't do it with heavy blitzes, which could've at least given Odunze some potential 1-on-1 opportunities for big plays either.

It's a key wrinkle on top of an already borderline flex play that keeps me off Odunze this weekend. ​
