item.title: Miami Dolphins’ painful season could be beginning of something special
item.description: Miami’s youth movement may pay big dividends moving forward.
item.content:encoded:
If we’re being honest, watching the Miami Dolphins in 2026 has not exactly been an enjoyable experience. The losses are piling up, the offense continues to struggle, and there are already rumblings from the team’s fanbase about the job head coach Jeff Hafley is doing.

But there is a silver lining to all of this, and it starts with the rookies.

Miami’s 2026 draft class is getting thrown into the fire, and that experience could pay significant dividends as the Dolphins move forward. Through five games, Hafley’s club leads the league in snaps from rookies, with over 2,000 such cases heading into their bye week. The Cleveland Browns are second — but are a staggering 600 snaps behind Miami in that department.

First-round offensive guard Kadyn Proctor has played 293 offensive snaps, appearing on 100% of Miami’s offensive plays. Second-round linebacker Jacob Rodriguez has logged 311 defensive snaps, while first-round cornerback Chris Johnson has played304 defensive snaps. Fifth-round safety Michael Taaffe isn’t far behind, with 287 defensive snaps to his name.

That’s a massive amount of responsibility for a group of players who were playing college football just months ago.

Rodriguez has already established himself as a major contributor in the middle of Miami’s defense — and is in the running for the NFL’s Defensive Rookie of the Year award. Johnson is getting valuable experience against high-end NFL receivers, while Taaffe is learning how to operate in a professional secondary. Proctor, meanwhile, is receiving the kind of weekly education that only comes from facing elite NFL defensive linemen.

Will they make mistakes? Absolutely. They’re rookies. But every missed assignment, every difficult matchup offers another opportunity to learn.

When the 2027 season rolls around, these players won’t be entering training camp as inexperienced newcomers trying to figure everything out. They’ll have an entire NFL season under their belts. They’ll understand the speed of the game, know what their coaches expect, and have a much clearer idea of what they need to do to improve.

That doesn’t guarantee they’ll become stars, but it gives Miami a chance to build around players who have already experienced the initial growing pains of a rebuild.

Now, imagine pairing that experience with a few quality free-agent additions. Miami currently has over $110 million in projected cap space for 2027 according to Spotrac.

The Dolphins won’t spend recklessly. Instead, they’ll pluck a couple of young, high-character standouts in search of a new home. General manager Jon-Eric Sullivan needs to identify a few difference-makers to add to his roster while allowing Miami’s young core the opportunity to continue to develop.

Of course, the Dolphins still have plenty to prove this year. But losing in 2026 doesn’t mean the season will be a complete waste.

Miami is finding out which young players can handle daunting NFL responsibilities, and those answers could prove invaluable moving forward. If Sullivan gets the next offseason right, this painful year could become the foundation for something special.

The Dolphins might not be ready to contend today, but the hope is that the experience these rookies are gaining now will help Miami get there a whole lot sooner than some expect.

Keep the faith. Trust in Jon-Eric Sullivan. Fins up.

item.title: Sean Payton has a simple request to get Broncos QB Bo Nix back on track
item.description: Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix said he's been "overanalyzing and overthinking things" this season. His coach has a simple instruction to fix that.
item.content:encoded:
To sum up his desires for his quarterback, Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton referenced a line from the award-winning television show, “The Bear.”

“Let it rip,” Payton told third-year quarterback Bo Nix, same as the note the main character found from his older brother to end the first season.

The phrase lends itself more to a Hollywood moment than an NFL quarterback making split-second decisions dozens of times over multiple hours. But to watch Nix in 2026 is to understand where Payton, who took play-calling duties back from offensive coordinator Davis Webb prior to the Broncos win over the Los Angeles Chargers on Oct. 11, is coming from.

“I’ve said to him, ‘Man, you’re the guy we wanted here, let’s go. You’ve done a ton of things well,’” Payton said. “But I think there’s a lot that goes into that.”

Nix and the Broncos (3-2) will go under the microscope in prime time Thursday with a tilt against the defending champion Seattle Seahawks (3-2), coming off a home loss to the San Francisco 49ers, in what could have been the Super Bowl matchup eight months prior.

One difference between then and now is that Nix has taken a step backward within the Broncos’ offense, according to ESPN analyst Dan Orlovsky. During the Oct. 12 edition of “NFL Live,” Orlovsky described “significant” regression in timing and rhythm.

“You can’t live in this type of NFL offense,” Orlovsky said. “There’s no timing and rhythm to, right now, his feel in structure in the passing game.”

With the tape rolling, Orlovsky pointed out Nix moving into pressure despite being provided a clean pocket.

“We did not see this from him (in the past),” Orlovsky said.

There is still a disconnect between Nix and the QB he is and the QB he is trying to be/they want him to be in @Broncos#nfllivepic.twitter.com/RzBfhzVWTV

— Dan Orlovsky (@danorlovsky7) October 13, 2026

According to Next Gen Stats, no quarterback in the league throws from further back in the pocket than Nix, who at 9.05 yards of average depth upon his release is nearly a half-yard deeper than the next-closest quarterback (Caleb Williams, 8.58 yards).

Those aren’t the only damning numbers for Nix, Webb – stripped of play-calling duties four games into the assignment – and Payton. The Broncos averaged 3.7 yards per rush and 4.6 yards per pass attempt against the Chargers. Denver's offense (-11.1 expected points added) turned in its second-worst marks of the season in EPA per play and success rate.

Simplifying his process is a way he can improve, Nix told reporters this week. He’s on board with the “let it rip” mentality.

“Let’s play fast, and let’s roll,” the 26-year-old said. “I think sometimes I can have a tendency of overanalyzing and overthinking things, and that’s when I’m not at my best. I want to have all the answers and get everything right, and it’s too difficult – eleven guys moving on defense, it’s tough to always figure it out. I do think I can make the game simpler and just get back to, ‘One, two, checkdown,’ that sort of thing and making sure my reads are on point.”

Payton is aware that there are throws not being made that could lead to chunk plays, which his why he’s publicly encouraging his quarterback to let loose. He knows that Nix will have to rely on his play-making skills if the opposing defense takes away his reads as he moves through a standard progression.  

“We’re always trying to find those plays that are clean, that kind of unfold versus the coverage you want,” Payton said. “To answer your question, a lot of it, you’re really paying attention to the game you’re in too, relative to risk. I think that that’s something that his experience, certainly at Oregon, has helped him.

“It’s bumpy. We’re constantly grinding to calm it down and create some matchups in some – call it first or second in the progression throws, that make it less risky."

By that, Payton means he doesn’t always want his quarterback to play like their team is trailing by 17 in the fourth quarter, “where now you’re playing in a different type of game relative to the throws you’re making.”

“So, there is that happy medium I think,” Payton said.

Nix reiterated that he is confident in his preparation, the Broncos’ coaching and the talent around him. He finished 16-of-27 passing against Los Angeles for 123 yards and a touchdown with no interceptions, but two fumbles (one lost).

“It’s just playing each play as it comes,” Nix said. “When it’s there, hit it.”

In Nix’s mind, a few extra plays being made over the first five weeks of the season that would flip the perception of his performance. He’s been reminding himself that playing hero ball isn’t always the right play – and that the answer is often in front of him.

“Next thing you know, stat line looks different,” Nix said.

He’s also grappling with the reality that mistakes happen. No quarterback can be perfect.

“At the end of the day, who cares? … Just play the play,” Nix said.

Wide receiver Courtland Sutton was quick to acknowledge the pressure facing Nix. For the Broncos to experience the success they want, Sutton said, “we need (Nix) to be able to have that success.”

“You ask any of the guys in the locker room, everyone has that same mentality of wanting to have each other’s back,” Sutton told reporters. “Especially when it comes to (Nix), I think that we all have that mentality of wanting to make sure that he feels comfortable, confident to be able to go out there and play fast.”

Nix understands that confronting critiques is part of the gig.

“Playing good, playing bad, it’s a narrative, and I think it’s honestly something we kind of make up,” Nix said.  

Media folks have a job to do too, he added.

"I guess sometimes they can say whatever they want and unfortunately, I can’t say whatever I want back,” Nix said with a laugh.

Nix can talk with his play, though – starting in prime time against the defending champs.

item.title: Week 6 NFL Survivor strategy and picks
item.description: David Fucillo provides NFL Survivor pool tips in Week 6, offering up safe, value, and trap picks.
item.content:encoded:
Week 6 is upon us! The playoff picture is slowly taking form, but there’s still a lot to sort out midway through October.

Three teams remaining undefeated. The 49ers beat the Seahawks and the Vikings beat the Saints to each improve to 5-0. The Chiefs are 4-0 and coming out of their Week 5 bye. On the other side of things, the Dolphins, Titans, and Chargers all lost last week to drop to 0-5. The Chargers were expected by many to compete for the AFC West title, but that isn’t happening.

Week 6 gets underway on Thursday with the Seahawks and Broncos facing off in Denver. An unexpectedly interesting matchup will see the 3-2 Browns hosting the 4-1 Ravens with significant AFC North implications. The 3-2 Raiders host the 4-1 Bills with AFC implications if Las Vegas can rebound from two straight losses to the Chiefs and Patriots. The Bengals, Lions, Dolphins, and Vikings all have their bye this week.

I’m back with my week 6 Survivor picks ahead of Seahawks-Broncos on Thursday Night Football. Survivor involves picking one team each week to win. If they win you advance, if they lose you’re out in most cases. I’m in one pool with four entries, but it’s also a double-elimination pool. I lost one entry after taking the Chargers and Bucs the first two weeks. Last week I took a first loss in a couple other entries thanks to my decision to take the Cowboys on Thursday. I’ve got three entries alive with one strike against each.

Below I’ve got a look at the safest choices, best value picks, and then trap picks. I’ll post my own picks at the end. I’ll update on Sunday once I lock in my three picks for the weekend.

I’ve included odds for the favorite in each game, courtesy of FanDuel.

Safest picks

Rams (-12.5) over Cardinals
49ers (-7.5) over Commanders
Patriots (-7.5) over Jets

The Cardinals stink and LA should have no problem with them. The Rams haven’t exactly impressed this season, but they also faced a rough first five games on the schedule. They head into a five-game stretch in which they very well could win all five with relative ease.

The Commanders have Jayden Daniels back, but considering what we saw against a not great Giants team, this could be an ugly one for them.

Best value picks

Rams (-12.5) over Cardinals
Patriots (-7.5) over Jets

You could save the Rams for any of the next four games, but this feels like the most winnable of those games. You could also save the Patriots for Week 8 on the road against the Dolphins or Week 18 at home against the Dolphins, but you need to get to that point in the first place.

Trap pick

Chiefs (-8.5) over Chargers

I went with divisional games above, but while the Cardinals clearly are not a good team, I remain convinced the Chargers could still prove dangerous. You can find tremendous value down the line with the Chiefs, as they have home games against both the Jets and the Cardinals later this season.

My picks this week

I’ll be taking two Rams picks this week. My third pick, I’m leaning Patriots, but we’ll see.

item.title: The Detroit Lions are getting back ‘a top-10 center’ in Cade Mays
item.description: One Carolina Panthers analyst told us the Detroit Lions have a top-10 center in Cade Mays.
item.content:encoded:
As soon as next game, the Detroit Lions will finally get to see what they’ve got in free agent signing Cade Mays. Detroit invested a three-year, $25 million contract in Mays, only to see their biggest offseason addition suffer a fractured wrist in training camp. But with his practice clock already started, there’s an expectation Mays could take the starting center position as soon as Detroit’s next game against the Green Bay Packers.

A couple weeks back—as part of our Pride of Detroit Direct “First Byte” podcast—we talked to Panthers analyst and radio host John Ellis to preview the Lions vs. Panthers game. Toward the end of the show, we picked Ellis’ brain about Mays and how he played in Carolina for the past few years. Needless to say, he’s a big fan of Mays.

“You guys will be thrilled with everything he brings to the table,” Ellis said. “On the field, he’s a mauler in the run game, he can climb to the second level, he’s got great anchor ability in the pass game. He’s not without flaws, but he’s a top-10 center in my book in this league. And he’s been a big liability in terms of his loss here in Carolina. He’s also a funny dude off the field, and a great follow on social media. So, you’ll love him. He’s a Dan Campbell guy. When I saw Dan got Cade Mays, I said, ‘Shit, that’s perfect, man.’”

One of the most important roles Mays will eventually fill is a pre-snap diagnoser. NFL centers must do their best to read the defense’s pressure looks, adjust the protection accordingly, and communicate that to the entire team. Even though Mays has only been at the center position for a couple of seasons, Ellis believes that’s another strength in his game.

“He plays with intensity and leadership, and he is tremendous in terms of anchoring the center, not just physically, but also commanding everything in terms of the checks, pre-snap stuff,” Ellis said. “He’s a very refined player in that department.”

Of course, all of that begs the question: Why did the Panthers let him go? In Ellis’ opinion, it was simply a matter of finances.

“They had to make a business decision, and I think it was pretty clear that they were going to have to move on. They drafted Sam Hecht last year, and Luke Fornter is a stop-gap,” Ellis said.

Earlier in the week Lions coach Dan Campbell noted that while they’re going to get Mays some time during the bye week to continue to work out and get ready to return to the field, there are still some decisions that have to be made with how the offensive line will shake out vs. the Packers. That’s especially true considering backup center Juice Scruggs has been playing well in Mays’ absence.

“It’s going to be nice to get Cade in the mix. And look, so much of this is, we’ve got to see exactly where he’s at,” Campbell said. “We’ve got basically two days of half practices with him and so let’s see what it looks like next week. He’s going to continue to train here and then we got to make a decision on how do we work this. That’s what’s a little unique, he plays center. It’s not like you’re rotating a guard. So how do we handle this? What’s the best way? Can he go 70 reps? So, there’s a lot of factors that go into it right now.”

Regardless, at some point Mays will take his spot at center, and the Lions offensive line—which is already one of the best in football—could take the next step.

item.title: Four wide receiver trades the Steelers should make
item.description: Four WR trades the Pittsburgh Steelers should make.
item.content:encoded:
The Pittsburgh Steelers enter Week 6 without three of their wide receivers. Michael Pittman is on IR with a foot injury, and both Roman Wilson and Ben Skowronek suffered injuries in the Steelers’ Week 5 win over the Colts that will leave them unable to play against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

That leaves DK Metcalf, Germie Bernard, and Kaden Wetjen as the only receivers who made the initial 53-man roster that are healthy. Brandon Smith was called up on Sunday, and may get a roster spot in Week 6. Should the Steelers want to make a splash, though, and add a proven playmaker, there are multiple names to look at via trade.

Vikings WR Jauan Jennings

Jennings signed with the Vikings this past offseason after five seasons with the San Francisco 49ers. He put up solid numbers over his last two seasons, with 55 receptions in 2025 and 77 catches in 2024. Thus far with Minnesota, he has just two receptions for nine yards. Considering his proven ability to do the underneath nitty-gritty stuff, including hard run blocking and catching passes through contract, he fits what Pittsburgh wants to do offensively. A 2028 fifth-round pick in exchange for his services would be a good move for Pittsburgh to make.

Titans WR Calvin Ridley

Ridley is in his ninth NFL season, and his current role with the Tennessee Titans is a small one. He has only caught five passes on eight targets thus far in 2026. Ridley isn’t far removed from a pair of 1,000-yard seasons in 2023 and 2024, and perhaps playing in a better offense with a quarterback like Aaron Rodgers would bring out a bit of the player we saw a few seasons ago. He’ll be 32 before the season ends. With that in mind, A 2028 sixth-round pick would be fair compensation for the former Second-Team All-Pro.

Browns WR Jerry Jeudy

Do I think the Browns will trade Jeudy to the Steelers while both are very much alive in a playoff race? No. But if we only wrote about things we think will happen, not a lot of work would get done. It’s far from unprecedented to see players dealt within the division. The Browns traded quarterback Joe Flacco to the Bengals last season, and Mike Tomlin was infamously really, really fine with it. Jeudy caught 50 passes a season ago, but only has eight catches on 15 targets in 2026. Shipping a fifth-rounder to Cleveland for the 27 year-old wouldn’t be the worst idea.

Jaguars WR Brian Thomas

We saw Marvin Harrison Jr get dealt to the Houston Texans in a splash move, which leaves Thomas as the biggest name being centered around trade rumors at the position. The 2024 Pro Bowler has gotten lost in the pecking order due to Parker Washington emerging as a budding star, as well as Jakobi Meyers and Brenton Strange being the second and third options in the Jaguars’ offense. After nearly 1,300 yards in 2024, injuries saw that number dip to just over 700 in 2025. Through five games, he has nine catches for 105 yards. A third-round pick may be enough to secure a deal for Thomas, who would instantly become the best receiver on the team.

Let us know what you think in the comments. Be sure to bookmark Behind the Steel Curtain for all the latest news, breakdowns, and more!

item.title: Ultimat Fan: It comes down to Bo
item.description: It’s been a few short days since the Broncos pulled out a win over a hapless Chargers team, and in less than 24 hours, they will be trying to do it again. Except this time, the opponent is the defending Super Bowl champs with its revitalized journeyman quarterback throwing to last season’s Offensive Player of […]
item.content:encoded:
It’s been a few short days since the Broncos pulled out a win over a hapless Chargers team, and in less than 24 hours, they will be trying to do it again.

Except this time, the opponent is the defending Super Bowl champs with its revitalized journeyman quarterback throwing to last season’s Offensive Player of the Year. Thankfully, the Seahawks no longer carry their Super Bowl MVP running back, Kenneth Walker III, on the roster, but the defensive challenge remains high.

Both teams are 3-2, but Denver enters the home matchup with a lot of questions about its offense and defense. And here to help us answer them before kickoff is veteran UFGer, OrangeAndBlueFan, who absolutely nails it on the first question.

Mile High, you better be loud because this game could come down to the real “12th Man” fans pulling out the dub for the Throwback Broncos (my fave)!

Week 6: Seahawks at Broncos on TNF

MHR – This week’s matchup has the Broncos coming off a fortunate win against a team in shambles. How in the world does Denver beat Seattle?
OrangeAndBlueFan: It’s a short week against the defending champs. This isn’t a week to reasonably expect the Broncos to fix much of anything from a scheme standpoint. They win the same way they beat Jacksonville and the Rams (and were right there with a chance to do against the 49ers, but failed). The defense plays well enough to prevent the game from getting out of hand early, and we all sit around and wait for the three second half drives that look like the 2013 Broncos out of the blue. Then take our heart medication and spend the next 10 days talking about how terrible our 4-2 team is.

The other possibility is the issue with Bo is more mental than physical. He’s in his head. He’s thinking about too much instead of just playing instinctually. I think playing a Thursday night game might actually help him. Sean Payton has said before that, for Thursday games, you have to install a simplified game plan because of the lack of prep time. I think that helps someone who is stuck in their head and struggling as a result, and I think with a simplified game plan we might actually see a competent NFL offensive operation Thursday night.

MHR –  Third down conversions were a gigantic issue in the Chargers game, converting just once on 12 third-down tries.  Is this a fixable problem? How do we do it – scheme, protection, better play calls?
OrangeAndBlueFan: Someone correct me if I’m wrong, I don’t have stats to back this up, but I feel like third down conversions have been an issue for 2.5 seasons now. Aren’t we leading the league in three-and-outs again this year (or at least very close)? I’m firmly in the camp that third down isn’t actually the problem, first down is. The Broncos are abysmal on first down. I think the solution is to gain more than two yards on first down. But it’s not like the Broncos don’t know this and aren’t trying. Dobbins looks broken, and as valuable as Harvey is as a pass catcher, he’s not a good between the tackles runner. Maybe the answer is Jonah Coleman, which doesn’t help us this week. Maybe the answer is George Paton picking up the phone – Tyler Allgeier, perhaps (he’s someone I was hoping we’d target in free agency)? Also doesn’t help us this week. Maybe it’s more designed runs for Bo. Maybe it’s more quick, short passes. I honestly don’t know, but something needs to change on first down, which will have a trickle down effect to third down.

MHR –  Denver’s “expected points added” metric ranks among the worst in the NFL at 24, and while Wil Lutz provided 12 of the 23 points last week, he also missed a 42-yarder. What is going on with this offense; they switched play callers and got an early touchdown and then still stalled? 
OrangeAndBlueFan: I would caution against putting too much stock in metrics like “expected points added.” This, along with many other “advanced” or “next gen” stats, is relatively new to football, and most of them are actually unproven yet, in terms of if they reliably predict success or failure (we’ve all heard the phrase “correlation doesn’t equal causation.” right? It takes a long time for a new analytic to prove that it is predictive and not just correlative).

That point aside, yes, it’s obvious to anyone with a functioning brain that the Broncos offense is not good. I never thought the issue was playcalling. I think that was just an easy lever for Sean Payton to pull to try to turn things around, so he did. The problem is we have a quarterback who isn’t seeing the field and is failing to step up into clean pockets and deliver the football to wide open receivers down the field, and we have a virtually non-existent running game. In the wise words of Pepper Brooks, “that’s a bold strategy, Cotton, let’s see if it pays off.”

Are these problems fixable? Yes, I believe they are. But I wouldn’t count on that in a Thursday night game with no practice and prep time during the week

And you mentioned Lutz – I am quite concerned with how shaky he’s looked so far, with the 42 yarder in L.A. being a pretty egregious miss. 50+ yard misses can be forgiven (as long as you also make some, which Lutz hasn’t yet this year, I don’t believe), but you start missing chip shots and your leash before we’re trying out other kickers at Wednesday practice is going to get a whole lot shorter.

MHR – The Broncos’ O-line has been good in spurts but often does not seem ready or able to protect Bo. How does this offensive line win in the trenches against Seattle’s front four?OrangeAndBlueFan: I don’t care how good an offensive line is, when your opponent knows you are passing the ball, it’s going to be difficult to stop their pass rush. If we’re not able to gain more yards on first down, I’d expect to see more of the heavy packages we started to see the last two games. I don’t love that that typically means we’re only sending two receivers out on routes, but if that’s what is needed to give Bo the confidence to climb a pocket and throw the ball with confidence, that’s ok. When Bo plays with sound mechanics and fundamentals, I fully trust him to deliver accurate footballs into tight windows. And if the passing windows aren’t there, but Bo actually climbs the pocket, that opens up the middle of the field for him to run, which is where he is truly dangerous.

MHR – The run game was showing more promise (stop me if you have heard this before) with Jonah Coleman, but since his injury it has once again seemed…lackluster. While Coleman is on IR, do you think RJ Harvey and JK Dobbins can carry this rushing attack? Can it be something that opponents actually have to put resources into defending? Why is our run game always so mediocre?
OrangeAndBlueFan: Let me stop you, I’ve heard this before! Lol. No, I don’t think Harvey and Dobbins can carry the run game. Harvey has never been a good inside runner, and Dobbins is either injured or not very good anymore. The run game was actually good on a per carry basis last year before Dobbins got injured, but Payton didn’t call enough run plays. This year it seems like we’re doing a little better in calling more run plays, but the team isn’t able to execute them at a high level.

No, if I was Seattle, I would do the same thing every other team has done against Denver. Sit back in two high safety and force the Broncos to have success running the ball, all along knowing that they can’t. If I’m the Broncos, I’d maybe try a few zone read concepts, but tell Bo to keep the ball. I have noticed numerous times this year that Bo frequently makes the wrong read on the zone read plays. He very rarely keeps the ball himself, and very often should.

MHR – The offseason addition of Jaylen Waddle was supposed to be a huge spark for our offense, and it has barely been a flicker. Waddle was visibly frustrated on the field last week over a missed third down conversion on a run, but he hasn’t been exactly contributing to an improved offense. What do you make of the low number of throws to Waddle and Courtland Sutton – our WR1 and 2 – and where is the blame…on Bo Nix? On the play calls? On the receivers for drops?
OrangeAndBlueFan: There’s no way of knowing for sure without being at Dove Valley during the week and knowing the exact scheme and play designs, but I think this is primarily on Bo. He’s not seeing the field well and is straight up failing to throw the ball to open guys down the field. That said, Waddle certainly has no room to point fingers at other people. He’s been good for a drop per game, and often on what would have been an explosive play, too. He could probably have 5 more catches for 120 more yards on the season if he caught everything that hit him in the hands. And that’s not to mention the snowball effect of making those catches – continuing a drive after an explosive play, rather than punting back to the other team after another 3 and out. We might even be having a completely different conversation about Bo if Waddle didn’t have bricks for hands. The crazy thing about football, from an analysis standpoint, is that everything is always based on small sample sizes. It doesn’t take a huge number of plays going differently to completely change your analysis of a player’s performance, and I think Waddle’s drops this year have been a little overlooked in how much they’ve likely contributed to Bo’s story so far this season.

I have no idea what is going on with Court. It was great to see him get the touchdown Sunday in L.A., because he’s been invisible. I haven’t noticed him ever getting open, which is surprising considering he isn’t being covered by the opponent’s top DB anymore. I wouldn’t mind Payton calling a few plays on Thursday to just simply force feed Sutton the ball. Not just for Sutton, but also for Bo. Court has been Bo’s security blanket for the first two years of his career. You want to get a professional athlete out of a slump? Start by putting him in comfortable, familiar situations. Sean Payton has mountains of plays that are designed to scheme receivers open. Call a series of those plays that is designed to get Sutton open, and tell Bo to step up into the pocket and throw it out there where #14 can catch it, and trust him to do his job. Call some of those back shoulder throws down the left sideline that they were so good at connecting on last year. Call some of those 20 yard in-cutting routes they were so good at connecting on Bo’s rookie season. I really think Sutton is the key to getting things turned around for Bo.

MHR – We’ve talked about Denver’s running backs and wide receivers, so against this dominant and fast Front 7 that has one of the better win rates on the pass rush and ranks near the top on takeaways, what kind of offensive scheme can the Broncos put together to mitigate Seattle’s strengths and minimize their own offensive weaknesses?
OrangeAndBlueFan: I don’t know enough about the X’s and O’s of football to give a great answer to this question – maybe this is a good one to call on Broncos Country to chime in in the comments. What I will keep going back to is we need to find a way to generate more positive yards specifically on first down. Whether that’s more shallow slants or mesh routes, zone reads with Bo using his legs instead of always handing it off, or jumbo packages to get an extra blocker in the run game. I’m not really an expert here and don’t know what would be most likely to work. But also, it’s a Thursday game, so realistically I’m not sure we are going to see anything different. I really think the defense is just going to have to keep it close until Bo morphs into Tom Brady in the 4th quarter.

MHR – Fans and analysts have both been souring on Bo Nix the last few weeks. Are you concerned about the QB not being as good as we hoped/assumed or is it just a matter of the still young QB having to play a lot of tough defenses out of the gate this season?
OrangeAndBlueFan: I understand the angst with Bo. He was looking like a good NFL QB by the end of last season, and our hope was that he would come into year 3 and grow from there. It hasn’t worked out that way, and the offense is tough to watch. But I’m not ready to bail on Bo yet. His basic stats (attempts, yards and touchdowns) through 5 games last year weren’t that much better than they are through 5 games this year, and he’s played against much tougher defenses this year, with perhaps the toughest test still to come Thursday. I need to see him get to play the likes of Arizona, Carolina and Miami before I panic and start talking about Bo not being the Broncos long-term QB. Until it still looks like this against teams of that caliber, I’m still ridin’ with Bo. In the infamous words of Terrell Owens, that’s my Quarterback!

And besides, what are the alternatives? We’re still 3-2 against tough competition, with a very favorable schedule on the horizon. This is very likely going to be a playoff team with a late draft pick, so no better option at QB there. There aren’t going to be great free agents at the QB position this offseason. And does Broncos Country really have the appetite for another Russell Wilson-like trade? It’s gotta be Bo. He’s gotta improve. And with what I expect will be a simplified game plan on Thursday, followed by a much easier slate of opponents, I think he will.

Could this also be a whole lot of hope, without much evidence, because the notion of what happens if Bo isn’t “him” is nauseating to think about? Sure, also possible. We’re just fans. We don’t control any of this. So I’m absolutely going to continue burying my head in the sand as long as the Broncos continue finding ways to win ugly!

All of this said, there is a combination of two stats that definitely have my attention. Bo ranks 31st in the NFL in completion percentage AND ranks 33rd in average depth of target. Those are stats that should be inversely correlated. To be the worst in the league at both is definitely concerning, and something that could quickly change my mind about Bo if at least one of those numbers doesn’t improve significantly in pretty short order. 

MHR – The Broncos will still be missing Pat Surtain II and now Talanoa Hufanga on Thursday. How do the Broncos defensive backs slow Jaxon Smith-Njigba, the reigning Offensive Player of the Year, who gained over 100 yards on the Niners defense last week? 
OrangeAndBlueFan: I think most people’s first instinct would be to say heavy zone defense. I really don’t like that idea. Our defense is terrible in zone, JSN will find the holes, and might run all the way back to Seattle. Honestly, I think the answer might be to sacrifice KAD to the man coverage gods, concede that JSN is going to have a monster game, and absolutely shut everything else the f down. If you can keep JSN to 150 yards and two scores, and make the rest of their offense look like a high school JV team, the Broncos win easily. If you can keep JSN to 200 yards and 3 scores, while making the rest of their offense look like a high school JV team, the Broncos still have a good chance to win. As I mentioned earlier, I’m not an X’s and O’s expert here, so this might be an absurd idea, too. My issue is that I just don’t see the defense having an answer for JSN without PS2 and Hufanga out there, so why use multiple resources trying and failing, when those resources could be used to completely stonewall everything else and make Seattle totally one dimensional.

MHR – In the Seahawks loss to the Niners last week, Sam Darnold threw one touchdown but also two interceptions and only 195 yards passing overall while kicker Jake Meyers was responsible for 12 of Seattle’s points. What can the Broncos’ defense learn from the Niners’ scheme against the Seahawks?
OrangeAndBlueFan: Related to my last answer, Seattle’s offense is very one-dimensional and will turn the ball over. Instead of using resources on trying to stop the one explosive weapon they do have, concede that he’s going to get his, and focus our efforts on keeping them one-dimensional. The Broncos have very clearly made generating turnovers a priority this year, and are having some success there. I expect to see a high effort in attacking the football on defense Thursday. The more time JSN spends sitting on the bench, the better the Broncos chances of winning. The most effective way to maximize JSN’s bench time is to turn the ball over.

On the other side of things, Seattle’s defense is definitely good, but they aren’t perfect. Let’s not forget they gave up 33 points to a backup QB in a loss to Washington just a few weeks ago. They are get-able. It all comes down to Bo being able to settle his feet down (and likely settle his mind down) and step up into clean pockets so he can deliver accurate throws down field. At the end of the day, I firmly believe that is what will determine the outcome of this game.

MHR – The Broncos defense has seemed slow to bring effective pressure this season but it has been better at getting takeaways. Can Nik Bonitto, Que Robinson, Jonah Elliss and the edge group get home often enough to make Darnold make mistakes the defense can capitalize on? What’s the key?
OrangeAndBlueFan: I’d love to see more from Ellis and Bonitto, but Zack Allen is the key. Darnold is not a mobile QB, but he is good at navigating within the pocket. Interior pressure is kryptonite for a QB like Darnold. This could also be a good game for VJ to show off his creative chops with a lot of stunts designed to open pass rushing lanes for Strnad or McMillan to get to Darnold. I don’t think the edge rushers need to great for the pass rush to be effective against a QB like Sam Darnold….. But it sure would be nice to see Bonitto start rolling, and for Ellis to…. well….. do anything at all (Ellis has been one of the bigger disappointments on the defensive side of the ball this year, in my opinion).

MHR – Which ONE player on offense and ONE player on defense has to be an MVP on Sunday for the Jets to win? Which one offensive and defensive player for the Broncos are you
OrangeAndBlueFan: For the Seahawks, it’s Holani (or whoever their main RB ends up being). If they can establish a run game against us, game over. Defensively for Seattle, I don’t know enough individual players to name one, but it’s their pass rush. The Broncos can win if Bo can get his feet and his mind right and calmly step up into the pocket. If they can prevent him from doing that, the Broncos could be in for a long night.

For Denver, offense is easy. It’s Bo. He will almost single-handedly determine who wins this game. On defense, I’m still going to stick with Zack Allen. I think there’s a case for the linebackers getting turnovers, but I’m going with Allen. Consistent interior pressure in the pocket could totally wreck the game for Seattle.

Predictions

Stats for BO NIX?   1 win, and I’ll leave it at that!

Stats for SAM DARNOLD?  21 of 31 for 258 yards and 3 touchdowns. 5 sacks. 2 game-altering fumbles.

Stats for each running back?   Dobbins: 14 carries for 48 yards and one touchdown. Harvey: 3 carries for 11 yards, 6 receptions for 45 yards and a touchdown. Badie: 2 carries for 7 yards, 2 receptions for 13 yards. Nix: 3 carries for 22 yards.

Stats for each receiver/TE?  Waddle: 7 catches for 96 yards. Sutton: 6 catches for 59 yards. Franklin: 3 catches for 18 yards. Mims: 1 catch for 12 yards. Engram: 2 catches for 16 yards and a touchdown. Trautman/Other: 2 catches for 14 yards. So, to give a real answer for Bo’s stats above, let’s just add it up: 29 completions (on let’s say 43 attempts) for 273 yards and 3 touchdowns. No turnovers.

Longest FG from Lutz this week?   49

Number of sacks to Sam Darnold?  5

Number of sacks to Bo Nix? 1

Who gets the first sack of the game for the Broncos? 99, all day!

Who gets the most sacks? I think Allen gets 2 

Who gets a pick-six?  I think we force 2 or 3 fumbles, but no picks.

How many INTs/FF/FR for the Seahawks D?    0/0/0

How many INTs/FF/FR for the Broncos D?  0/3/2

How many penalties between the two teams?   17

Final Score? I’m not going to just give the score, I’m going to predict how this plays out:

The state of the offense through 5 games doesn’t give me a ton of confidence that the Broncos will win this game. That said, I also don’t feel a lot of confidence picking a team that has to travel on a short week to altitude to play a prime time game at Mile High. But this isn’t asking for confidence, it’s asking for a prediction. I think a simplified short week game plan helps Bo get out of his own way, and things look better offensively in the first half.

Defensively, however, the Broncos have no answer for JSN with PS2 and Hufanga out, and Smith-Njigba goes for over 175 yards and 3 scores in the first three quarters of the game. Despite the Broncos offense finally looking competent, Seattle takes a 24 – 17 lead into the 4th quarter…….

And then, 4th quarter Bo shows up, the effects of traveling to altitude on a short week begin to take its toll on the Seahawks, and Mile High Magic does what it does best (there’s no atmosphere in sports quite like the 4th quarter of a prime time game at Mile High). Broncos win the 4th quarter 10 – 0, to win the game 27 – 24 and improve to 4-2, before getting to face one of the easiest schedules in the NFL over the remainder of the season. Bo plays well enough to back people away from the ledge, and we enter the mini-bye talking about the possibility of home games in January instead of whether or not we have a franchise QB.

Wishful thinking? Perhaps. But what fun is being a fan if you can’t dream about what could be? (*editor’s note: I love this!)

The Favorites 

Favorite Broncos win ever with John Elway? I’m not originally from Colorado and didn’t become a Broncos fan until after Elway retired. I’ll go with the Super Bowl win over the Packers. I never was a Brett Favre fan, and I always appreciated Elway and wanted to see him get a ring. I remember watching that game and rooting for Denver.

Favorite Broncos game ever with Peyton Manning? SB50, even though PFM was just along for the ride at that point in his career. Nothing better than an all-time great winning a Super Bowl in the last game of his career.

Favorite Broncos game ever with any other QB? 2005 (January 2006) divisional round win over New England (see details below)

Team you love to beat the most in the AFC? Kansas City

Coach you despise most in the NFL? Nick Siriani(not sure if spelling is correct)

Team you hate to lose to the most in the AFC?  Pittsburgh, outside of the division anyway

NFC team you could cheer for in the Super Bowl?  New Orleans, Detroit, L.A., San Francisco. And yes, Dallas (see below). Wow, there are a lot of NFC teams I lowkey like.

NFC team you’d want to face more than any other in the Super Bowl? I want Thursday to be a Super Bowl preview. I want revenge on Seattle.

Toughest game remaining on the schedule?  Buffalo

Favorite Broncos player on your current roster?  PS2

Favorite new guy/rookie on the team?  Waddle should be the easy answer at this point, but it hasn’t panned out that way so far. So I’ll say Coleman by default.

Food/Snack you have to eat on game day?  Mostly copied and pasted from last year: I have season tickets with a friend and we tailgate for a few hours before every home game. We alternate weeks cooking, and do it up right! So it isn’t the same every week, but it’s ALWAYS good eats! This is only our fifth year with tickets, but trying to one-up the previous week with our tailgate food has quickly become a tradition!

Favorite game analyst/commentator? Greg Olsen or J.J. Watt

How did you become a Broncos fan?

(Copied and pasted from last year):

I was an adult before I became a Broncos fan addict. I was born in New Orleans and grew up in Dallas during the Cowboys 90’s dynasty. So I was a Cowboys fan as a kid, and the Saints were my #2. I ended up in Denver for college in 1999, but I was playing on a golf scholarship so my Sundays were always spent either practicing or traveling to tournaments, so I didn’t really follow football for those 4 years.

After college, I stayed in Colorado and started following football again, but had lost any feeling of loyalty to the teams I grew up rooting for. Colorado was the first place I lived that really felt like home to me, so it felt really natural to start rooting for the Broncos. By the time I attended my first ever NFL game in person – the 2005 playoffs (January 2006) win over the Patriots – I was already a Broncos fan, but that game was basically a life changing experience, and I’ve never looked back since.

Getting to be live in that environment for Champ’s 100 yard pick 6 on Brady was the most electric, jaw on the ground, hair standing up on the back of my neck moment I’ve ever experienced watching sports.

item.title: Patriots opponent preview: Are the Jets quietly growing into a contender?
item.description: Players to watch, stats, injuries, and more for the Patriots’ opponent on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
Sunday’s game between the New England Patriots and New York Jets will be a meeting between two second-year head coaches who have enjoyed differing levels of success so far. Whereas Mike Vrabel led the Patriots to the Super Bowl in his first season and appears to have his team firing on all cylinders again in 2026, Aaron Glenn went just 3-14 in Year 1 and is also currently the owner of a losing record.

That said, could it be that the Jets are quietly building a contender? There are some arguments for it, so let’s take a closer look at the 2-3 team before its trip to face the 3-2 Patriots.

Jets key stats

The Jets are currently below .500 and outside the AFC playoff picture, but a look at their statistics reveals that there are some areas of their team that can compete with any other in football.

If we look solely at the statistics as presented, one could expect a fairly defensive-dominated battle between two of the best such units in football. The Jets’ is indeed just that, and well-rounded despite being in the middle of the pack in the turnover category (that said, the group did caught its first interception since 2024 earlier this year). That being said, New England’s offense — which scored 74 points over the last two games — is as formidable an opponent as it has faced thus far.

The Jets’ offense, meanwhile, has had its issues and has been unable to perform at the same level as its defensive counterpart. The group has limited its own errors as evidenced by its three giveaways all year, but it nonetheless ranks in the bottom half of the league in most other major categories.

Jets 2026 season

For the first time since 2023, the Jets opened a season with a win again. However, the momentum they built in Week 1 quickly started to fade again: the club lost three straight afterwards.

Week 1: 23-10 win at Tennessee Titans (1-0)
Week 2: 20-17 OT loss vs. Green Bay Packers (1-1)
Week 3: 31-24 loss at Detroit Lions (1-2)
Week 4: 23-12 loss at Chicago Bears (1-3)
Week 5: 17-12 win vs. Cleveland Browns (2-3)

While three straight losses to NFC North opponents turned a 1-0 start into a 1-3 record, the Jets are entering a crucial meeting with the Patriots off of their most impressive win thus far. Sure, their offense scored only 17 points and fumbled twice, but their defense registered eight sacks, two fumble recoveries of its own, and limited what was a 3-1 Browns team to a mere 198 yards of offense and 3.0 yards per play.

So, are the Jets quietly growing into a contender as asked above? They do have a relatively easy schedule ahead of them and some talented pieces on both offense and defense, but one has to wonder about their ceiling given their rather uninspiring offensive performance so far.

Jets active roster

Roster up-to-date as of Oct. 15, 5 a.m. ET | *denotes nominal starter

Quarterback (2): Geno Smith* (7), Cade Klubnik (10)

Running back (4): Breece Hall* (20), Braelon Allen (0), Isaiah Davis (32), Kene Nwangwu (3 | KR)

Fullback (1): Andrew Beck (47)

Wide receiver (5): Garrett Wilson* (5), Adonai Mitchell* (15), Isaiah Williams (18 | PR), Tim Patrick (17), Malik McClain (84)

Tight end (4): Mason Taylor* (85), Kenyon Sadiq* (16), Jeremy Ruckert (89), Jelani Woods (86)

Offensive tackle (4): Olu Fashanu* (74 | LT), Armand Membou* (70 | RT), Max Mitchell (67), Chukwuma Okorafor (79)

Interior offensive line (5): Dylan Parham* (64 | LG), Josh Myers* (71 | C), Joe Tippmann* (66 | RG), Jordan Meredith (67), Kohl Levao (60)

Interior defensive line (5): Harrison Phillips* (97), T’Vondre Sweat* (99), Jowon Briggs (91), Darrell Jackson Jr. (95), Jack Heflin (96)

Defensive edge (5): David Bailey* (31), Kingsley Enagbare* (52), Will McDonald IV (9), Joseph Ossai (46), Nate Lynn (92)

Linebacker (4): Demario Davis* (56), Jamien Sherwood* (44), Trevin Wallace (49), Kiko Mauigoa (51)

Cornerback (6): Azareye’h Thomas* (1), Brandon Stephens* (21), Jarvis Brownlee Jr.* (2), D’Angelo Ponds (23), Qwan’tez Stiggers (37), Nahshon Wright (26)

Safety (4): Minkah Fitzpatrick* (29), Dane Belton* (6), Andre Cisco (8), Malachi Moore (27)

Specialists (3): Jason Sanders (19 | K), Austin McNamara (14 | P/H), Thomas Hennessy (42 | LS)

After spending the last few years watching the Zach Wilson, Aaron Rodgers and Justin Fields experiments go up in flame, the Jets continue to be stuck in quarterback purgatory. Their latest QB investment arrived via a trade with the Raiders in March: Geno Smith joined the team that had originally drafted him in 2013 alongside a seventh-round draft pick in exchange for a sixth-rounder.

That trade alone should tell you what Smith’s market and by extension his level is at this point in his career. Under normal circumstances, he would be a bridge quarterback, but with the Jets that bridge continues to lead nowhere (or to fourth-round rookie backup Cade Klubnik, which could effectively be the same).

As for Smith himself, he is still capable of playing at a decent level even at age 36. So far this year, he has completed 102 of 147 pass attempts for a 69.4% completion rate, 1,084 yards, six touchdowns and no interceptions. That said, he has lost more sack yards than any quarterback in the NFL through five weeks (134), is ranked only 17th in net yards per attempt (5.8), and 19th in expected points added per play (0.048). He is capable of steering the vehicle, but has yet to show he can successfully maneuver it around some more challenging obstacles.

Smith is surrounded by a talented supporting cast, though. The offensive line is bookended by former first-round draft picks Olu Fashanu and Armand Membou; Breece Hall and Braelon Allen are a solid 1-2 punch at running back; Mason Taylor and first-round rookie Kenyon Sadiq are the same at the tight end position.

And then, there is Garrett Wilson. A bona fide No. 1 wide receiver, Wilson has caught 31 passes for 374 yards and three touchdowns — leading the team in all three categories and accounting for roughly one third of the team’s arial production.

As opposed to the Jets’ offense, the defense is lacking the same high-end star power. That said, as a unit is much more cohesive and has been a lot more productive so far. A lot of it is due to a player who already is looking like he face of the operation on that side of the ball: first-round draft pick David Bailey, who has five sacks and a forced fumble in five career games and appears to be a legitimate NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year candidate.

Bailey, Kingsley Enagbare and Will McDonald are a formidable edge trio supported by a stout interior led by Harrison Phillips, T’Vondre Sweat and Jowon Briggs. Together, the group has proven itself disruptive against both the pass and the run.

At linebacker, Demario Davis still leads the group even at age 37. He and Jamien Sherwood, who is 11 years younger, are both capable of playing at a high level from a physical and mental perspective.

In the secondary, Azareye’h Thomas is building on a solid rookie season and now a starter on the outside and the team’s quasi-CB1. Veteran safety/offseason signing Minkah Fitzpatrick, meanwhile, caught that aforementioned interception in Week 4 to become the first Jet to pick off a pass since Week 18 of the 2024 season. It remains New York’s only INT to date.

In the kicking game, Austin McNamara has gotten plenty of work in: he leads the league with 25 punts. Jason Sanders, meanwhile, is a combined 15 of 17 on field goals and extra points. Isaiah Williams is averaging a very good 10.9 yards per punt return.

Jets reserves

Practice squad (17): QB Will Levis (4), RB Al-Jay Henderson (36), WR Jamaal Pritchett (81), WR Sterling Shepard (87), OT Brant Banks (75), OL Nick Dawkins (53), OL Jimmy Morrissey (65), DT Isaiahh Loudermilk (58), DT Payton Page (98), ED Quinton Bell (—), ED Paschal Ekeji (54 | exempt), ED Nathan Voorhis (57), LB Jaden Keller (48), LB Troy Reeder (50), CB Mory Bamba (38), CB Jordan Clark (33), CB Samuel Wormack (22)

PUP (1): ED Tyler Baron (94)

The Jets’ reserve lists include one of their first-round draft picks this year, wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr. The 30th overall pick in this year’s draft suffered an ankle injury in Week 1. Like the Patriots’ A.J. Brown, he too returned to practice on Wednesday to open his 21-day window to return to the active roster.

Jets coaching staff

Head coach: Aaron Glenn

Coordinators: Frank Reich (OC), Brian Duker (DC), Chris Banjo (ST)

Aaron Glenn joined the Jets alongside general manager Darren Mougey last offseason, and the two have since amassed a 5-17 record together. They also oversaw significant change on the. coaching staff this offseason, with both coordinators — Frank Reich and Brian Duker — hired this offseason to replace the departed Tanner Engstrand and Steve Wilks.

item.title: Packers RB Josh Jacobs' status in limbo as video release delayed
item.description: Packers RB Josh Jacobs has missed five games while the NFL investigates his domestic violence incident, but police are delaying release of key video evidence.
item.content:encoded:
As the Green Bay Packers prepare for their sixth consecutive NFL game this season without star running back Josh Jacobs, neither the team nor the NFL have offered updates on Jacobs' return, and Wisconsin police are temporarily withholding video that could aid the league's investigation.

Jacobs was arrested after a domestic dispute with his ex-girlfriend at his home in May and ultimately charged with two misdemeanors, one for battery and one for criminal damage to property. Although he reached a plea deal in September, Jacobs remains on the NFL commissioner's exempt list, a form of paid leave that prohibits him from practicing or attending games, while the league determines Jacobs' potential punishment under the league's player code of conduct. 

Packers head coach Matt LaFleur said on Oct. 12 the team had received no updates from the league on Jacobs' status. That same day, an NFL spokesperson told USA TODAY Sports in an email, "The matter remains under review of the personal conduct policy. There’s no timeline."

Meanwhile, Wisconsin police are delaying the release of video evidence cited in the criminal investigation into Jacobs' alleged domestic assault to requesting parties, including the NFL and USA TODAY Sports.

Josh Jacobs video unsealed but unreleased

Jacobs' ex-girlfriend had asked the court to seal all evidence in the case, including surveillance camera footage of the May 23 incident. But on Sept. 24, Brown Circuit County Court Judge Marc Hammer lifted the temporary seal order and ruled that the Hobart-Lawrence Police Department had discretion, "to apply a balancing test between the rights of the public, the defendant and the victim in deciding whether to release the records."

USA TODAY Sports submitted a public records request for the video to the Hobart-Lawrence Police Department on Sept. 28. In a letter to USA TODAY Sports dated Oct. 13, Hobart-Lawrence police chief Michael Renkas wrote that police determined they could release some records with "appropriate redactions," but cannot not do so yet because attorneys for the record subjects – presumably Jacobs and his ex-girlfriend – intend to seek judicial orders restraining disclosure.

"Accordingly, the Department is temporarily withholding all responsive records in accordance with the statutory waiting period and any applicable court orders," Renkas wrote. "This temporary hold does not constitute a denial of your request or a reversal of the Department's balancing-test determination."

The NFL also reportedly filed a public records request seeking access to the video, according to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport.

According to Renkas' letter, Hobart-Lawrence police also "provided courtesy notification of its intent to release additional records, including police reports, body-worn camera recordings, and squad camera recordings" in Jacobs' case.

Renkas cited a statute in Wisconsin state law, § 19.356, concerning records obtained through subpoenas and search warrants. The law requires authorities to inform people in writing within three days after making the decision to permit access to such records pertaining to them. The record subject then has 10 days to file a court order seeking to restrict access to the records, and if they do so, the authority cannot release the records until the court's final decision, which could take up to 30 days and is subject to appeal.

Wisconsin does not have a strict statutory deadline for responding to public records request, instead mandating that agencies must fulfill or deny a request "as soon as practicable and without delay."

Jacobs' ex-girlfriend's attorneys previously argued that the sealing of evidence is within her rights under Marsy's Law – a recently added amendment to Wisconsin's state constitution that gives additional rights to victims of a crime – to protect privacy, dignity and safety.

Will the NFL suspend Josh Jacobs?

According to the NFL's 2025 personal conduct policy, players can be subject to discipline by the league even if their conduct does not result in criminal charges or a conviction.

The NFL conducts its own investigation separate from law enforcement and attempts to interview all parties, including alleged victims, though the league does not have subpoena power and cannot force cooperation from people who are not players or league employees.

Sometimes, delays in legal proceedings or the release of law enforcement records can slow down the NFL's investigatory process – as is the case in Jacobs' situation.

A standard suspension for a domestic violence case is six games, according to the collective bargaining agreement between the NFL and NFLPA, but suspensions can be longer depending on the severity of the case.

Jacobs has been on the commissioner's exempt list since Aug. 30. His time on the commissioner's exempt list could retroactively count toward a suspension if the NFL decides to impose one as punishment after its investigation concludes.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Packers RB Josh Jacobs' status in limbo as video release delayed

item.content:encoded:
Whether it’s big-time throws being made by quarterback Patrick Mahomes or gashing runs by running back Kenneth Walker, the Kansas City Chiefs’ offense looks like one of the NFL’s best once again after a multi-year stretch when that was not the case.

But what’s different about this version of the Chiefs offense?

The latest Kansas City Chiefs news

The Chiefs’ offense has been elite again — but for an entirely different reason | The Kansas City Star

Here’s the oddity of the biggest change they made: They were basically the worst under-center team in the NFL a year ago. They totaled just 45.1 yards per game in the formation, second-to-last in the league. They averaged 3.0 yards per pass attempt while lining up under center, last in the league.

Then they decided to do more of that.

And what do you know, a year later, they lead the NFL in rush yards per play (6.3) in under-center formations, a half-yard better than second place, and rank second in pass yards per play (9.5), more than triple the efficiency of last season.

Chiefs still have faith in pass rush, despite going without a sack since Week 1 | ESPN

Entering this week, the Chiefs ranked 27th in pass rush win rate, generating pressure by beating the opponent’s pass protection within 2.5 seconds just 45% of the time. The concern for the Chiefs after their most recent game, a comeback win over the Las Vegas Raiders, is that quarterback Kirk Cousins, who they pressured on just 34.6% of his pass drops, was the least mobile passer they have faced so far this season.

“We’ve done a good job of keeping the quarterback busy back there, though, with pressure, which is important,” coach Andy Reid said Monday. “Hands down, we want to have sacks. But the pressure on the quarterback ends up being an important thing, and I think our guys have been generating that.”

Cyrus Allen and 7 more Kansas City Chiefs players who should play a bigger role after the Week 5 bye as injuries reshape the roster | A to Z Sports

Briningstool has been the clear No. 3 tight end behind Travis Kelce and Noah Gray. His pass blocking leaves something to be desired (one pressure allowed on just two pass-blocking attempts), but he’s proven to be one of the team’s better run blockers at the position. In fact, he leads all Chiefs tight ends in run-blocking grade, according to Pro Football Focus. That includes both Gray and Kelce.

With the running game becoming a much bigger part of the offense, getting your best run-blocking tight end on the field more often makes sense. Also, don’t put it past Kansas City to lean into more 13-personnel play-action looks. Briningstool made some acrobatic catches during training camp and the preseason.

The story behind Chiefs rookie’s hot start? A Patrick Mahomes DM — and question to the GM | The Athletic

Kansas City Chiefs general manager Brett Veach was in the Blum Student Union cafeteria lunch line when rookie running back Emmett Johnson caught him off guard.

Johnson asked a direct question — and one Veach acknowledges now he wasn’t fully prepared for.

“Y’all don’t think I can block, do you?”

Chiefs Emerge as Potential Candidate for Week 8 Primetime Flex | Heavy Sports

The Philadelphia Inquirer recently noted that the NFL is considering flexing the Eagles-Washington Commanders matchup out of “Sunday Night Football” in Week 8, as both teams currently have losing records.

John Breech of CBS Sports examined the league’s other alternatives for the coveted primetime slot, but doesn’t believe there is a good option. Here is his case against the Chiefs-Broncos being flexed.

Around the NFL

Micah Parsons explains cautious return to play, doesn’t ‘care’ he’s missing Cowboys-Packers game | NFL.com

“The biggest thing that people worried about with me, they’re like, ‘Man, why ain’t he back yet?’” he said this week on “The Edge with Micah Parsons” podcast. “If the Super Bowl was this week, I’m playing in the Super Bowl. But it’s just about me making sure I have all the small things fixed first.”

Parsons underscored that the main concern isn’t injuring the repaired ACL again, but rather all the things that could go wrong by pushing to return early.

Jaguars are first team since the merger not to allow a 40-yard rusher in first five games | Pro Football Talk

Last year, the most rushing yards any player gained in a game against the Jaguars was 74, by Colts running back Jonathan Taylor. The Jaguars have now gone 23 consecutive games, counting last year’s playoff game, without allowing a 75-yard rusher.

Opposing running backs have totaled 83 carries for 210 yards against the Jaguars this season, an average of just 2.5 yards per carry. That’s by far the best defense against running backs in the NFL this season.

Lamar Jackson has ‘realistic chance’ to return vs. Browns in Week 6 | CBS Sports

Jackson battled several nagging issues last year. Officially, an early-season hamstring injury cost him three games, and a back bruise caused him to miss another game late in the year. Unofficially, Jackson rarely looked like his normal explosive self. He had just 67 carries for 349 yards, both career lows, and his 5.2 yards per carry was his lowest mark since his rookie year, when he took over as starter midseason. Jackson’s pocket mobility evaporated, too, as he had a career-high sack rate.

In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride

Patrick Mahomes sees how the Chiefs’ offense can take it to the next level

“It was easy once I saw Kenneth running the football,” Mahomes reflected about the offseason. “I was like, ‘We have to make sure we give him the best chances to succeed.’”

“Obviously, he has run the ball terrific under center, and the offensive line has taken it upon themselves to fire off the ball and get that stuff down,” Mahomes continued. “I knew if we were able to do that, the play action game would open up even more. Then it’s about me just being the best quarterback for this team. It’s always going to be different, and this team was about being under center, getting him going and then play action off of it. I’m sure the defenses will adjust, and we’ll adjust off of that as well.”

item.title: Breaking down Seahawks RB depth chart without Price, Charbonnet
item.description: The Seahawks lost Kenneth Walker III in free agency and now have a new-look RB depth chart. Here's what to know about their top running backs.
item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Seahawks lost Super Bowl 60 MVP Kenneth Walker III to the Kansas City Chiefs in 2026 free agency.

Seattle invested a first-round pick in Notre Dame product Jadarian Price to help replace him. The idea was to have Price work in tandem with Walker's long-time foil, Zach Charbonnet, and create a solid one-two punch at running back.

So far, that dream hasn't materialized. Charbonnet hasn't yet played while recovering from a torn ACL suffered during Seattle's Super Bowl run. Meanwhile, Price was placed on injured reserve (IR) before Week 4 because of a chest injury.

That has led the Seahawks to utilize a handful of lesser-known running backs to open the 2026 NFL season. Here's what to know about Seattle's running back rotation, when Price and Charbonnet could return and why the team considered signing Joe Mixon to a contract.

Who is the Seahawks starting RB?

Emanuel Wilson is serving as the Seahawks' starting running back with Price and Charbonnet out of the lineup. The 27-year-old signed with the Seahawks as a free agent after spending his first three NFL seasons with the Green Bay Packers.

Wilson went undrafted out of Fort Valley State in 2023 and originally signed with the Denver Broncos as a free agent. After a three-day tenure in Denver, Wilson landed in Green Bay and eventually established himself as a solid backup for the Packers. He racked up 242 carries for 1,083 yards and seven touchdowns over his three years with the Packers, appearing in 41 games with two starts.

The Seahawks thought highly enough of Wilson (5-10, 226 pounds) to give him a one-year deal worth just under $1.6 million. He was expected to be a backup in Seattle but has comported himself well in the wake of the team's injuries, generating 301 total yards and three touchdowns on 78 touches.

Wilson figures to continue as Seattle's lead back until either Price or Charbonnet can return to the lineup.

Seahawks RB depth chart

The Seahawks have three healthy running backs on their 53-man roster. They are as follows.

  1. Emanuel Wilson
  2. George Holani
  3. Robert Henry Jr.

Holani has served as the complement to Wilson amid Seattle's running back injuries. The fourth-year veteran has generated just 77 yards on 26 carries but has been better as a pass-catcher, logging 11 catches for 76 yards. He is Seattle's preferred third-down back because of that and his blocking abilities.

Meanwhile, Henry, an undrafted rookie, hasn't yet played a snap for the Seahawks since being signed off the Washington Commanders' practice squad ahead of Week 5. He was inactive against the San Francisco 49ers, with veteran Velus Jones Jr. serving as Seattle's third-string running back.

Jones was cut from the 53-man roster ahead of Week 6 and signed to the practice squad. It isn't clear whether he will be elevated to continue in his role as the third-stringer or if Henry will eventually be granted the opportunity to operate in such a role.

The Seahawks also have Dontae McMillan, an undrafted rookie from Eastern Michigan, on their practice squad.

While the Seahawks have an established pecking order at running back for now, it could change considerably once their top players return to the lineup.

Jadarian Price injury update

Price was placed on IR with a chest injury ahead of Week 4. Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald referred to Price's injury as an "aggravation" of a previous chest problem when he was placed on IR.

The good news for Seahawks fans? Price isn't expected to be out for the season, as Seattle general manager John Schneider said in an Oct. 4 appearance on Seattle Sports.

Schneider said in that interview the team doesn't "see (Price's injury) as a season-ending thing at all," though he declined to put a definitive timeline on the rookie running back's return.

Still, Price will not be eligible to return to the field until Week 8 at the earliest.

Zach Charbonnet injury update

Charbonnet remains out of action for the Seahawks while continuing to recover from a torn ACL.

Macdonald said ahead of Week 6 that Seattle was not planning to have him available against the Broncos. He also implied the team was taking a measured approach with the 25-year-old running back's return.

"We have to have consensus from all parties that he's ready to go," Macdonald said of Charbonnet. "That he's the most confident and ready to go. That he's had enough exposure to go play an NFL game. Those are the variables at play here."

While Charbonnet isn't playing in Week 6, ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reports the veteran has a "legitimate chance" to suit up in Week 7 against the Kansas City Chiefs.

Is Joe Mixon on the Seahawks?

The Seahawks were originally going to sign Mixon to their practice squad after Price's injury. However, Seattle decided not to go through with the signing after the veteran running back underwent a physical with the team.

Mixon missed the entire 2025 NFL season while dealing with the aftermath of a "freak" foot injury. The two-time Pro Bowler, who rushed for 1,016 yards in 2024, remains unsigned.
